n.0: "Bad" is irregular; "baddest" is not standard in formal English.
n.1: "Most worst" is a double superlative; "worst" already means "most bad."
n.3: "Worse" is the comparative, used for exactly two items.

GR.q: Which sentence contains a pronoun with no clear antecedent?
o: In the brochure, it says that flu shots are free.
Dr. Ames said she would give the flu shots herself.
The brochure says that flu shots are free for staff.
The clinic posted its flu-shot hours on the door.
GR.w: "It" has no noun to refer to; the brochure is the source, so name it: "The brochure says..."

n.1: "She" and "herself" both clearly refer to Dr. Ames.
n.2: The brochure is named as the subject, so no pronoun needs an antecedent.
n.3: "Its" clearly refers to the clinic.

GR.q: Which revision of "The nurses told the patients that they would be moved to the new wing" makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The nurses told the patients, "You will be moved to the new wing."
The nurses told the patients that they would be moved to their new wing.
The patients were told by the nurses that they would be moved to the new wing.
The nurses told the patients that they would all be moved to the new wing.
GR.w: In the quotation, "you" can only mean the patients, the people being spoken to, so the reference is clear.

n.1: "They" and "their" could each mean the nurses or the patients.
n.2: Switching to the passive voice keeps "they" with two possible antecedents.
n.3: Adding "all" leaves "they" pointing to either the nurses or the patients.

GR.q: Which sentence about a disaster shelter is capitalized correctly?
o: The American red cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last Winter.
GR.w: Every main word of an organization's name (American Red Cross) and a specific place (Lake Michigan) is capitalized; seasons are lowercase.

n.0: All main words in the organization's name are capitalized: "Red Cross".
n.1: "Lake" is part of the proper name "Lake Michigan", so it is capitalized.
n.3: Seasons such as winter are common nouns and are lowercase.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the comma splice in "The patient felt dizzy, however, she refused to sit down"?
o: The patient felt dizzy; however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, she, however, refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, however she refused to sit down.
GR.w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

n.1: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.
n.2: Moving "however" inside the second clause still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma.
n.3: A comma before "however" still joins two independent clauses with only a comma: a comma splice.

GR.q: Which sentence from a unit report contains a pronoun-antecedent agreement error?
o: The lab coats were returned, but it had not been washed.
The volunteers signed in and picked up their name tags.
The twins brought their own snacks to the checkup.
Mercy Hospital posted its new visiting hours online.
GR.w: "Coats" is plural, so the pronoun must be plural: "they had not been washed."

n.1: This sentence is correct: "volunteers" is plural and "their" is plural.
n.2: This sentence is correct: "twins" is plural and "their" is plural.
n.3: This sentence is correct: the hospital is one organization, so "its" agrees.

GR.q: Which sentence from a clinic door sign is punctuated correctly?
o: Patients who arrive after the doors close must use the side entrance.
Patients who arrive, after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
Patients, who arrive after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
Patients who arrive after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
GR.w: "Who arrive after the doors close" is essential: it tells which patients must use the side entrance, so it takes no commas.

n.1: "After the doors close" is part of the essential clause, so it is not set off with commas.
n.2: Commas would make the clause nonessential, so the sign would tell every patient to use the side entrance.
n.3: A comma must not separate the long subject from its verb "must use."

GR.q: Which sentence about clinic equipment uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
o: The binders on the top shelf have lost their colored labels.
The new infusion pump arrived, but they are missing a cord.
Each of the monitors on the unit needs their screen cleaned.
The scale and the monitor in Room 2 need its batteries replaced.
GR.w: "Binders" is plural, so the plural pronoun "their" agrees with it.

n.1: "Pump" is singular, so the pronoun must be "it is missing a cord."
n.2: "Each" is singular and refers to things, so the pronoun must be "its screen."
n.3: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their batteries."

GR.q: Which sentence from a student handbook draft has parallel structure?
o: The applicant was praised for her punctuality, her empathy, and for being skilled.
The checklist asks staff to wash hands, wear gloves, and dispose of sharps safely.
Volunteers may greet visitors, deliver flowers, or they can read to patients.
The course teaches students how to splint a fracture and controlling bleeding.
GR.w: All three items after "to" are base verbs (wash, wear, dispose), so the series is parallel.

n.0: Two nouns ("her punctuality," "her empathy") are followed by a gerund phrase with a repeated "for"; it should be "and her clinical skill."
n.2: The first two items are verb phrases, but the third is a full clause ("they can read"); it should be "or read to patients."
n.3: "How to splint" is paired with the gerund "controlling"; it should be "how to splint a fracture and control bleeding."

GR.q: Which sentence quoting a nurse is punctuated correctly in US style?
o: The nurse said "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "Take this with food", and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "take this with food," and handed me the cup.
GR.w: In US style, a comma separates the dialogue tag from the quotation, the quoted sentence begins with a capital letter, and the comma after the quotation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.0: A comma is needed after "said" to introduce the quotation.
n.1: US style places commas inside the closing quotation mark, not outside.
n.3: A quoted full sentence begins with a capital letter: "Take".

GR.q: Which sentence uses "who's" and "whose" correctly?
o: Who's the patient whose chart is missing?
Who's the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient whose chart is missing?
Whose the patient who's chart is missing?
GR.w: "Who's" is the contraction of "who is" (Who is the patient?); "whose" shows possession (whose chart).

n.1: The chart belongs to the patient, so the possessive "whose" is needed, not "who is".
n.2: The sentence opens with "Who is the patient", so it needs the contraction "who's".
n.3: Both are reversed: the opening needs "who's" and the possessive needs "whose".

GR.q: Which sentence uses the correct form of an irregular verb?
o: She has wrote three care plans for the pediatric rotation.
I seen the updated schedule posted near the break room.
By the time I arrived, my preceptor had went to the meeting.
The new aide has already taken the medication safety course.
GR.w: "Take" is irregular: take, took, taken. A helping verb ("has") takes the past participle "taken."

n.0: "Has" needs the past participle "written"; "wrote" is the simple past.
n.1: "Seen" is a past participle and needs a helping verb ("have seen"); otherwise use the simple past "saw."
n.2: "Had" needs the past participle "gone"; "went" is the simple past and cannot follow a helping verb.

GR.q: Which sentence from a nurse's journal punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
GR.w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.3: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".

GR.q: Read the sentence: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
GR.w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.1: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.
n.2: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."

GR.q: Which sentence about training for new aides uses parallel structure?
o: New aides learn to take vital signs, record intake, and reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, to record intake, and how to reposition patients.
New aides learn taking vital signs, to record intake, and repositioning patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, recording intake, and to reposition patients.
GR.w: Items in a series must share one grammatical form. After "learn to," the three base verbs (take, record, reposition) are parallel.

n.1: The third item switches from an infinitive ("to record") to a "how to" phrase, so the list is not parallel.
n.2: The list mixes gerunds ("taking," "repositioning") with an infinitive ("to record").
n.3: "Recording" is a gerund placed between two infinitives, which breaks the parallel pattern.

GR.q: In the sentence "The surgeon's hands stayed remarkably steady during the long operation," what part of speech is the word "remarkably"?
GR.w: "Remarkably" modifies the adjective "steady," telling how steady, so it is an adverb.

n.0: A noun names something; "remarkably" tells to what degree.
n.1: "Steady" is the adjective; "remarkably" describes "steady," not a noun.
n.2: The verb is "stayed"; "remarkably" shows no action.

GR.q: Which sentence from a clinic's flu-season update needs a comma added?
o: Patients could visit on weekday evenings or on Saturday mornings.
When flu season began, the clinic extended its evening hours.
By March, waiting times at the clinic had dropped by half.
The clinic hired two nurses and the staff shared the extra shifts.
GR.w: "The clinic hired two nurses" and "the staff shared the extra shifts" are independent clauses joined by "and," so a comma goes before "and." Without it, a reader first takes "two nurses and the staff" as one object.

n.0: This is one clause; "or" joins two phrases, so no comma is needed.
n.1: This sentence already has the comma after its introductory clause.
n.2: This sentence already has a comma after the introductory phrase "By March."

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The nurses gathered ___ in the lounge, but the meeting ran ___ too long."
GR.w: "All together" means as a group; "altogether" means completely.

n.0: The word meaning "completely" is one word: "altogether too long."
n.2: Both are reversed: gathering as a group is "all together," and "completely too long" is "altogether too long."
n.3: Gathering as one group is "all together," two words.

GR.q: Which sentence about a lost staff badge uses apostrophes correctly?
o: The nurses dont know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know who's badge was left in the lounge.
The nurse's don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
GR.w: "Nurses" is a plain plural (no apostrophe), "don't" is a contraction of "do not" (apostrophe where the o is missing), and "whose" is a possessive pronoun (no apostrophe).

n.0: The contraction of "do not" needs an apostrophe: "don't".
n.1: "Who's" means "who is"; the possessive needed here is "whose".
n.2: "Nurses" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe.

GR.q: In the sentence "Well, your blood pressure looks better than it did last week," what part of speech is the word "Well"?
GR.w: Set off by a comma at the start of the sentence, "Well" expresses a reaction and has no grammatical link to the rest of the sentence, so it is an interjection.

n.0: A conjunction joins words or clauses; "Well" joins nothing and stands apart at the start of the sentence.
n.1: "Well" is an adjective when it means healthy ("I feel well"); here it describes no noun.
n.3: "Well" is an adverb when it tells how something is done ("works well"); here it modifies no verb.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the punctuation error? "The discharge packet includes: a medication list, a follow-up card, and a diet sheet."
o: Replace the colon with a semicolon
Replace the colon with a comma
GR.w: A colon must not separate a verb (includes) from its objects. Deleting it lets the list follow the verb directly.

n.1: A semicolon cannot introduce a list or separate a verb from its objects.
n.2: A colon after "packet" would split the subject from its verb, which is also an error.
n.3: A comma must not separate a verb from its objects.

GR.q: Which word in the sentence is a preposition? "Although the clinic closes early, the lab stays open until six."
GR.w: "Until" takes the object "six" and has no verb after it, so it is a preposition showing time.

n.0: "Early" tells when the clinic closes, so it is an adverb.
n.1: "Although" is followed by a subject and verb ("the clinic closes"), so it is a subordinating conjunction.
n.3: "Open" follows the linking verb "stays" and describes the lab, so it is an adjective.

GR.q: Which sentence quoting a worried parent is punctuated correctly?
o: Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?".
Mrs. Diaz asked "is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished"?
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?"
GR.w: The quoted words are a question, so the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and it also ends the sentence; no second end mark is added.

n.0: The question mark already ends the sentence; adding a period doubles the end punctuation.
n.1: A comma should introduce the quotation, and the quoted sentence should begin with a capital letter.
n.2: The question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark.

GR.q: Which sentence from a history paper on nursing is capitalized correctly?
o: During the Civil War, many Irish Immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the civil war, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
GR.w: Named historical events (the Civil War) and nationalities (Irish) are proper nouns; general nouns such as immigrants are lowercase.

n.0: "Immigrants" is a common noun and is lowercase.
n.2: Nationalities are proper adjectives, so "Irish" is capitalized.
n.3: The name of a specific historical event is capitalized: "Civil War".

GR.q: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
o: Their new manager seems nicely, and the staff likes her a lot.
The coffee in the staff break room tastes bitter today.
The infant is breathing good now that the fever has broken.
The new bandage feels tightly around her swollen wrist.
GR.w: Linking verbs (taste, seem, feel, look, smell) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it: the coffee tastes bitter.

n.0: "Seems" is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective "nice," not the adverb "nicely."
n.2: "Breathing" is an action, so it needs the adverb "well," not the adjective "good."
n.3: "Feels" links the bandage to a description of it, so it takes the adjective "tight," not the adverb "tightly."

GR.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The volunteer ___ greeted us at the entrance has worked here for ten years."
GR.w: "Who" refers to people and is the subject of "greeted," so it is correct.

n.1: "Which" refers to things or animals, not to a person such as a volunteer.
n.2: "Whose" shows possession and would need a noun after it.
n.3: "Whom" is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of "greeted."

GR.q: Which sentence uses "lie" or "lay" correctly?
o: The dog has laid by the front door all afternoon long.
Please lie the clean linens on the bottom shelf of the cart.
After the procedure, the patient laid on his side for an hour.
Yesterday, Ana lay down for a nap after her long night shift.
GR.w: "Lie" (to recline, no object) is lie, lay, lain. "Yesterday ... lay down" is the past tense of "lie," so it is correct.

n.0: The dog is reclining, so the verb is "lie"; its past participle is "lain": "has lain."
n.1: Putting linens down takes an object, so the verb is "lay": "Please lay the clean linens."
n.2: The patient is reclining (no object), so the verb is "lie"; its past tense is "lay," not "laid."

GR.q: Which sentence about the crash-cart check uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither the students nor the nurse are checking the crash cart today.
The nurse, along with two students, are checking the crash cart.
The nurse, as well as two students, is checking the crash cart.
The nurse and two students, with the instructor, is checking the cart.
GR.w: Phrases such as "as well as," "along with" and "together with" do not make a subject plural. The subject is "nurse," so the verb is "is."

n.0: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurse," which is singular, so it must be "is."
n.1: "Along with two students" is an intervening phrase, not part of the subject. The subject "nurse" is singular, so the verb must be "is."
n.3: "The nurse and two students" is a compound subject joined by "and," which is plural, so the verb must be "are."

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Either the pharmacist or the two technicians ___ the refill requests each afternoon."
GR.w: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Technicians" is nearer and plural, so the verb is "check."

n.0: "Checks" agrees with "pharmacist," the farther subject; the nearer subject "technicians" is plural.
n.1: "Has checked" is singular and agrees with the farther subject, "pharmacist."
n.2: "Is checking" is singular; the nearer subject "technicians" needs "are checking."

GR.q: Which revision corrects the comma splice "The roads were icy, the clinic opened late" and shows cause and effect?
o: The roads were icy, the clinic, therefore, opened late.
Because the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
Although the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
The roads were icy, but the clinic opened late.
GR.w: Two steps: subordinating one clause fixes the splice, and "Because" signals cause and effect.

n.0: The two independent clauses are still joined by only a comma, so the splice remains.
n.2: "Although" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.
n.3: "But" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.

GR.q: In the sentence "The patient's heart was beating fast during the stress test," what part of speech is the word "fast"?
GR.w: "Fast" tells how the heart was beating, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb. The same spelling is an adjective in "a fast pulse," so the word's job decides.

n.0: "Fast" would be an adjective before a noun ("a fast heartbeat"); here it modifies the verb "was beating."
n.1: The verb is "was beating"; "fast" describes the beating.
n.3: "Fast" is a noun only when it names a period without food; here it tells how something happened.

GR.q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? "All visitors must ___ the hospital's mask policy."
GR.w: The standard idiom is "comply with" a rule or policy.

n.0: "Comply to" is a nonstandard idiom; the verb takes "with."
n.2: "By" belongs to a different idiom, "abide by"; "comply" takes "with."
n.3: "Comply for" is not a standard idiom.

GR.q: Which of these sentences is written in standard English?
o: Them forms need a signature from the patient or parent.
Irregardless of the forecast, the clinic will open at eight.
The clinic use to open at seven on weekday mornings.
The aide was supposed to restock the gloves before noon.
GR.w: "Was supposed to" is the standard written form: "supposed" keeps its -d ending.

n.0: "Them" cannot point to a noun; use "Those forms."
n.1: "Irregardless" is nonstandard; use "regardless."
n.2: The past-habit form needs the -d ending in writing: "used to open."

GR.q: Maria and Lee own one clinic together. Which sentence correctly shows their shared ownership of the clinic?
o: Maria and Lees' clinic opens at eight.
Maria's and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Marias and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Maria and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
GR.w: For joint ownership, only the last name takes the possessive: "Maria and Lee's clinic". Separate possessives (Maria's and Lee's) signal separate ownership.

n.0: Lee is one person, so the singular possessive is "Lee's", not "Lees'".
n.1: Making both names possessive signals individual ownership, which does not fit one shared clinic.
n.2: "Marias" is a plural with no apostrophe; Maria is one person and needs no s here.

GR.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "By the end of next May, Lena ___ all of her prerequisite courses."
GR.w: The future perfect (will have + past participle) shows an action that will be finished before a future time ("by the end of next May").

n.0: The past perfect marks an action before another past event, but next May is still ahead.
n.2: "Would have completed" belongs in a condition contrary to fact ("If she had enrolled, she would have completed..."); the sentence states a plan.
n.3: The present perfect connects the past to now; it cannot be finished by a future date.

GR.q: Which revision of "When the nurse set the vial on the tray, it cracked" removes the unclear pronoun reference?
o: When the nurse set the vial on the tray, they cracked.
The nurse set the vial on the tray, and it cracked.
The vial cracked when the nurse set it on the tray.
When the nurse set the vial on the tray, it suddenly cracked.
GR.w: With "the vial" named as the subject, "it" has one possible antecedent: the vial.

n.0: "They" has no plural antecedent and still does not say what cracked.
n.1: Joining the clauses with "and" keeps "it" pointing to either the vial or the tray.
n.3: Adding "suddenly" leaves "it" pointing to either the vial or the tray.

GR.q: A student quotes a nurse who said, "He refused the medication twice." The student wants to show that "He" means Mr. Diaz. Which version of the quotation is punctuated correctly?
o: "He, Mr. Diaz, refused the medication twice."
GR.w: Brackets mark words the writer inserts into someone else's quotation to clarify it.

n.0: Parentheses inside a quotation signal the speaker's own words, not the writer's insertion.
n.2: Commas would present "Mr. Diaz" as part of what the nurse said, changing the quotation.
n.3: [sic] marks an error in the original quotation; this quotation has no error and the name is still not added.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the faulty predication in "Hypoglycemia is when the blood glucose level drops too low"?
o: Hypoglycemia is where the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia, is a condition in which the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia is a condition in which the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia is a condition in which the blood glucose level drop too low.
GR.w: After a linking verb such as "is," the subject must be renamed by a noun phrase. "A condition in which..." renames hypoglycemia; "is when" (a time) and "is where" (a place) do not, so they are faulty predication.

n.0: "Is where" is still faulty predication: hypoglycemia is a condition, not a place.
n.1: The predication is fixed, but the comma now separates the subject (Hypoglycemia) from its verb (is).
n.3: The predication is fixed, but the singular subject "level" needs the singular verb "drops," not "drop."

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new exercise bike is ____, so it will ____ the walking program."
GR.w: "Stationary" means not moving; "complement" means to complete or go well with. A bike that stays in place goes well with a walking program.

n.0: "Stationery" is writing paper; a bike that does not move is "stationary".
n.2: "Compliment" means to praise; going well with something is "complement".
n.3: Both are wrong: the bike is stationary (not moving), and it complements (goes well with) the program.

MA.q: Which military time falls between 9:30 p.m. and 10:15 p.m.?
MA.w: 9:30 p.m. = 2130 and 10:15 p.m. = 2215. 2145 (9:45 p.m.) falls between them.

n.0: 1015 is 10:15 a.m., a morning time.
n.3: 0945 is 9:45 a.m.; p.m. hours need 12 added.

MA.q: A dosage calculation gives a volume of 3.96 mL, and the syringe being used is marked in tenths of a milliliter. What is 3.96 rounded to the nearest tenth? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.3.1: Rounded the 9 up to 10 but did not carry the 1 into the ones place.

MA.w: The tenths digit is 9. The hundredths digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so the 9 rounds up to 10, carrying 1 into the ones place: 3.96 → 4.0 mL (entered as 4).

MA.q: A multidose vial contains 20 mL of medication, and 4.5 mL has already been drawn from it. Each dose is 1.5 mL. How many more full doses can be drawn from the vial?
MA.w: Medication left: 20 - 4.5 = 15.5 mL. Doses: 15.5 ÷ 1.5 = 10.33. Only complete doses count, so round down: 10 full doses (10 × 1.5 = 15 mL; 0.5 mL is left over).

n.1: 14 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn and also rounds 13.33 up instead of down.
n.2: 11 rounds 10.33 up; 11 doses would need 16.5 mL, but only 15.5 mL is left.
n.3: 13 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn (20 ÷ 1.5 = 13.33, rounded down).

MA.q: A patient's oral temperature is recorded as 38.5 °C in the hospital chart. The patient's home thermometer reads in degrees Fahrenheit. What is the patient's temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This rounds 38.5 °C up to 39 °C before converting; round only at the end, and (9/5)(38.5) + 32 = 101.3 °F.
n.2: This adds the 1.5 °C gap between 37 °C and 38.5 °C straight onto 98.6 °F. A Celsius degree equals 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so the gap is 2.7 °F.
n.3: This multiplies by 2 instead of 9/5 (2 × 38.5 + 32 = 109); the factor is 9/5 = 1.8.

MA.q: A clinic filled 63 of its 84 appointment slots. What fraction of the slots was filled, in lowest terms?

n.0: 7/12 divides 63 by 9 but 84 by 7; dividing the terms by different numbers changes the value.
n.1: 9/12 divides both terms by 7 only; 9 and 12 still share a factor of 3.
n.3: 21/28 divides both terms by 3 only; 21 and 28 still share a factor of 7.

MA.q: Brand A oatmeal costs $5.28 for a 1.5-pound canister. Brand B oatmeal costs $4.60 for a 20-ounce canister. Which brand costs less per ounce, and by how much per ounce?
MA.w: 1.5 lb × 16 = 24 oz. Brand A: $5.28 ÷ 24 = $0.22 per oz. Brand B: $4.60 ÷ 20 = $0.23 per oz. Brand A is cheaper by $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This treats 1.5 lb as 15 oz. Since 1.5 lb = 24 oz, Brand A costs $0.22 per ounce.
n.2: This uses 12 oz per pound (1.5 lb = 18 oz); 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.3: $0.16 is the difference per pound ($3.52 vs. $3.68), not per ounce.

MA.q: A provider orders 30 mg of a medication. The vial is labeled 40 mg per 2 mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Round to the nearest hundredth.
MA.w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 30 ÷ 40 × 2 = 0.75 × 2 = 1.50 mL.

n.1: This divides by the 2 mL quantity instead of multiplying: 0.75 ÷ 2.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 40 ÷ 30 × 2 = 2.67 mL.
n.3: This stops at desired ÷ have (0.75) and does not multiply by the 2 mL quantity.

MA.q: A patient walks 850 m in the morning and 1.2 km in the afternoon. What is the total distance in kilometers?

n.0: This turns 850 m into 8.5 km (÷ 100) before adding.
n.1: This adds 850 m + 1,200 m = 2,050 m correctly but divides by 100 instead of 1,000.
n.3: This turns 850 m into 0.085 km (÷ 10,000) before adding.

MA.q: A school track measures 440 yards per lap. A student training for a fitness test wants to walk exactly 3 miles on the track. How many laps must the student walk? Enter the number of laps.

tr.4: Found the laps in one mile (1,760 ÷ 440) but not in 3 miles.
tr.36: Used 5,280 feet per mile with a lap measured in yards.

MA.q: At a pharmacy, Ana buys 3 bottles of vitamins at $4.79 each and 2 boxes of bandages at $12.65 each. She pays with a $50 bill. How much change should she receive?

n.0: $22.98 multiplies the vitamins by 3 but counts only one box of bandages.
n.1: $39.67 is the total cost, not the change.
n.2: $32.56 subtracts one bottle and one box ($4.79 + $12.65) instead of the full quantities.

MA.q: A scrub top regularly priced at $48 is on sale for 35% off. A 6% sales tax is then charged on the sale price. What is the total cost of the scrub top? Round to the nearest cent.

n.0: This combines the rates into one change (35% off and 6% on = 29% off, 48 × 0.71). Tax is charged on the sale price, so the multipliers 0.65 and 1.06 must be applied in turn.
n.2: This writes 6% as 0.006 instead of 0.06, so the tax comes out as about 19 cents instead of $1.87.
n.3: This is the sale price before tax; the 6% sales tax still has to be added.

MA.q: An infusion runs at 90 mL per hour. What is the rate in milliliters per minute?
MA.w: 90 mL/h × (1 h / 60 min) = 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 mL/min. The hours cancel, leaving mL per minute.

n.0: This multiplies by 60; the factor was set up with minutes on top, so the hours did not cancel.
n.1: This divides by 100, as if an hour had 100 minutes.
n.2: This divides 60 by 90, which gives minutes per milliliter, not milliliters per minute.

MA.q: A charge nurse spends 2/5 of her shift on direct patient care and 1/3 of the remaining time on charting. What fraction of the whole shift does she spend charting?
MA.w: After patient care, 1 - 2/5 = 3/5 of the shift remains. Charting takes 1/3 of that: 1/3 × 3/5 = 3/15 = 1/5 of the shift.

n.0: 1/3 is a fraction of the remaining time, not of the whole shift.
n.1: 2/15 takes 1/3 of the patient-care time (2/5) instead of 1/3 of the remaining time.
n.2: 11/15 adds 2/5 and 1/3, which treats both fractions as parts of the whole shift.

MA.q: A patient is to drink 3/5 of a 1 1/4-liter bottle of oral rehydration solution. How many liters should the patient drink?
MA.w: "3/5 of" means multiply. 1 1/4 = 5/4, so 3/5 × 5/4 = 15/20 = 3/4 liter.

n.0: 1 17/20 adds 3/5 and 1 1/4 instead of taking 3/5 of the bottle.
n.1: 1 3/20 multiplies only the fraction part (3/5 × 1/4 = 3/20) and keeps the whole 1.
n.2: 12/25 divides 3/5 by 5/4 (3/5 × 4/5) instead of multiplying.

MA.q: A health survey reports that 22.5% of adults in a county walk to work at least once a week. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equivalent to 22.5%?

n.0: 1/4 = 25%. It rounds 22.5% to 25% before converting, which changes the value.
n.2: 9/400 = 0.0225, which is 2.25%. The decimal point was moved one place too far.
n.3: 9/4 = 2.25. This writes the percent over 10 instead of 100.

MA.q: Which pair shows the same time in military and standard form?
MA.w: 0005 is 5 minutes after midnight, which is 12:05 a.m.

n.0: 1305 is 1:05 p.m.; nothing is added to the noon hour, so 12:05 p.m. is 1205.
n.2: 0005 is just after midnight, so it is a.m.; 12:05 p.m. is 1205.
n.3: 1205 is 5 minutes after noon, so it is 12:05 p.m.

MA.q: Three lab samples must total 10 g. Two of them weigh 3.75 g and 4.6 g. What must the third sample weigh?

n.0: 2.65 g forgets to reduce the ones digit after borrowing in 10.00 - 8.35.
n.3: 5.79 g lines up the last digits, adding 3.75 + 0.46 = 4.21.

MA.q: A 24-ounce bag of brown rice costs $4.56. A 2.5-pound bag of the same rice costs $7.20. Which bag costs less per ounce, and by how much?
MA.w: 24-oz bag: $4.56 ÷ 24 = $0.19 per ounce. 2.5-lb bag: 2.5 × 16 = 40 oz, and $7.20 ÷ 40 = $0.18 per ounce. The 2.5-lb bag is cheaper by $0.19 - $0.18 = $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This reverses the comparison; $0.18 per ounce is less than $0.19 per ounce.
n.2: $2.64 compares the bag prices, not the price per ounce.
n.3: $0.10 per ounce uses 1 lb = 10 oz (25 oz in the bag); 1 lb = 16 oz.

MA.q: A campus store buys a HESI A2 review book for $28 and marks it up 45% to set the retail price. During a sale, the store takes 20% off the retail price. What is the sale price of the book?

n.1: This takes 20% off the $12.60 markup only instead of off the full $40.60 retail price.
n.2: This is the retail price after the markup; the 20% sale discount still has to be applied.
n.3: This combines the changes as a single 25% markup (45% - 20%). Successive percents multiply: 1.45 × 0.80 = 1.16.

MA.q: Lena ran 3 3/10 miles on Monday and 2 4/5 miles on Tuesday. How much farther did she run on Monday?

n.1: 6 1/10 adds the two distances; "how much farther" needs a subtraction.
n.2: 1 1/2 subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger (8/10 - 3/10) instead of borrowing.

MA.q: A phlebotomist earns $27.50 per hour plus a flat $165 weekly bonus. Her pay for one week was $1,210, so 27.5h + 165 = 1,210. How many hours, h, did she work that week? Enter the number of hours.

tr.44: Divided 1,210 by 27.50 without first subtracting the $165 bonus.
tr.50: Added the bonus to 1,210 instead of subtracting it.

MA.w: Subtract the bonus from both sides: 27.5h = 1,210 - 165 = 1,045. Divide by 27.5: h = 1,045 ÷ 27.5 = 38 hours. Check: 27.5 × 38 = 1,045, and 1,045 + 165 = 1,210.

MA.q: A research protocol lists a vitamin supplement dose as 3 mg, but the lab's analysis software accepts doses in micrograms (mcg). Which value should be entered?
MA.w: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg (milli is 10⁻³ and micro is 10⁻⁶, a factor of 1,000 apart). Going from a larger unit to a smaller one, multiply: 3 x 1,000 = 3,000 mcg.

n.0: This is the number of micrograms in 3 g, not 3 mg (a factor of 1,000,000 is grams to micrograms).
n.1: This uses a factor of 100, as between meters and centimeters; milli and micro are a factor of 1,000 apart.
n.3: This divides by 1,000. Converting to a smaller unit gives a larger number, so multiply.

MA.q: What is 4/9 ÷ 2/3, in lowest terms?
MA.w: Keep the first fraction, change to multiplication, flip the divisor: 4/9 × 3/2 = 12/18 = 2/3.

n.0: 27/8 flips both fractions before multiplying.
n.1: 3/2 flips the first fraction instead of the divisor (9/4 × 2/3 = 18/12).
n.3: 8/27 multiplies 4/9 × 2/3 without flipping the divisor.

MA.q: A recipe for a heart-healthy breakfast bake calls for 2 2/3 cups of oats. A dietitian is making 1 1/2 times the recipe. How many cups of oats are needed?
MA.w: Convert to improper fractions: 1 1/2 = 3/2 and 2 2/3 = 8/3. Multiply: 3/2 × 8/3 = 24/6 = 4 cups.

n.1: 2 1/3 multiplies the whole numbers (1 × 2) and the fractions (1/2 × 2/3) separately; convert to improper fractions first.
n.2: 4 1/6 is the sum 1 1/2 + 2 2/3; scaling a recipe means multiplying.
n.3: 1 7/9 is 2 2/3 ÷ 1 1/2; the recipe is being increased, so multiply.

MA.q: Marcus's phone plan costs $35 per month plus $0.10 for each text message over 200. His bill for March was $47.40. How many text messages did he send in March?
MA.w: Let t = texts over 200: 35 + 0.10t = 47.40, so 0.10t = 12.40 and t = 124. Total texts sent = 200 + 124 = 324.

n.1: This subtracts the extra texts from 200 instead of adding them to 200.
n.2: This is the number of texts over the 200 included texts. The total sent is 200 + 124 = 324.
n.3: This divides the whole $47.40 bill by $0.10 without first removing the $35 monthly charge.

MA.w: Parentheses: 5 - 9 = -4. Multiply: -3 × (-4) = 12. Divide: 12 ÷ (-4) = -3. Subtract: 12 - (-3) = 12 + 3 = 15.

n.0: 9 makes 12 ÷ (-4) positive (12 - 3); a positive divided by a negative is negative.
n.2: -9 gives -3 × (-4) a negative sign (-12 + 3); two negatives multiply to a positive.
n.3: 0 subtracts 12 - 12 before dividing by -4; division comes before subtraction.

MA.q: A provider orders amoxicillin 375 mg by mouth. The pharmacy supplies amoxicillin oral suspension containing 250 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?
MA.w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 375 ÷ 250 × 5 = 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mL. As a proportion: 250 mg/5 mL = 375 mg/x, so 250x = 1,875 and x = 7.5 mL.

n.1: This inverts the dose ratio, using 250/375 × 5 instead of 375/250 × 5.
n.2: This divides 375 mg by 5 mL, as if each milliliter held 5 mg.
n.3: This divides the desired dose by the dose on hand but does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.

MA.q: An IV of 1,500 mL is ordered to infuse over 12 hours. After 5 hours, 700 mL have infused. At what rate must the rest of the IV run so that it finishes on time? Round to the nearest whole number.
MA.w: Volume left: 1,500 - 700 = 800 mL. Time left: 12 - 5 = 7 hours. Rate = 800 ÷ 7 = 114.29, which rounds to 114 mL per hour.

n.0: This divides the remaining 800 mL by the 5 hours already used instead of the 7 hours left.
n.2: This is the rate so far, 700 ÷ 5, not the rate needed for the remaining volume.
n.3: This is the original rate, 1,500 ÷ 12. The IV is ahead of schedule (700 mL infused instead of 625 mL), so 125 mL per hour for 7 more hours would deliver 1,575 mL and finish early.

MA.q: A 0.45-liter bottle of hand sanitizer costs $3.15. At this price, what is the cost per liter of hand sanitizer?
MA.w: Cost per liter = price ÷ liters: $3.15 ÷ 0.45 = 315 ÷ 45 = $7.00 per liter.

n.0: $1.42 multiplies $3.15 by 0.45 (1.4175) instead of dividing.
n.2: $0.70 moves the decimal point in 3.15 only one place when 0.45 is moved two places.
n.3: $0.14 divides 0.45 by 3.15, which gives liters per dollar.

MA.q: An architect builds a model of a new hospital wing at a scale of 1:200. The model is 45 centimeters tall. How tall will the actual building be, in meters? (1 meter = 100 centimeters)
MA.w: Each model centimeter represents 200 actual centimeters: 45 × 200 = 9,000 cm. Convert: 9,000 ÷ 100 = 90 meters.

n.0: This divides the model height by 200 instead of multiplying; the real building is larger than the model.
n.2: This divides 9,000 cm by 1,000 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.
n.3: This divides 9,000 cm by 10 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.

MA.q: A patient gained 4.15 pounds between two weekly weigh-ins. Which mixed number, in lowest terms, is equal to 4.15?
MA.w: The decimal part has two places: 0.15 = 15/100. Divide both terms by 5: 3/20. So 4.15 = 4 3/20.

n.0: 4 1/15 treats the digits after the decimal point as a denominator (4.0666...).
n.1: 4 3/10 = 4.3. It divides 15 by 5 but 100 by 10.
n.2: 4 3/200 = 4.015. It uses 1,000 as the denominator instead of 100.

MA.q: A patient drinks 0.24 L of juice, 0.6 L of water and 0.375 L of milk. What is the total intake in liters?
MA.w: Line up the points and fill with zeros: 0.240 + 0.600 + 0.375 = 1.215 L.

n.2: 1.115 L forgets the 1 carried from the hundredths column (4 + 7 = 11).
n.3: 0.405 L lines up the last digits instead of the decimal points.

MA.q: What is the value of the expression (8 - 2 × 5)² ÷ 4 + 6?
MA.w: Inside the parentheses, multiply first: 2 × 5 = 10, so 8 - 10 = -2. Square: (-2)² = 4. Divide: 4 ÷ 4 = 1. Add: 1 + 6 = 7.

n.0: 5 squares -2 as -4; a negative number squared is positive.
n.1: 0.4 adds 4 + 6 before dividing; division comes before addition.
n.3: 231 works left to right inside the parentheses ((8 - 2) × 5 = 30), then 900 ÷ 4 + 6.

MA.q: At a walk-in clinic, the number of evening appointments on Monday was 4 fewer than twice the number of morning appointments. If m is the number of morning appointments, which expression represents the number of evening appointments?
MA.w: 'Twice the number of morning appointments' is 2m. '4 fewer than' that amount means subtract 4 from it: 2m - 4.

n.0: '4 fewer than' a quantity means 4 is subtracted from that quantity, so the 4 comes second; 4 - 2m reverses the order.
n.2: This swaps the numbers: the morning count is doubled (multiplied by 2), and then 4 is taken away.
n.3: This subtracts 4 before doubling, which equals 2m - 8, not 4 fewer than twice m.

MA.q: A clinic orders 3 cases of syringes at $42.75 each and 5 boxes of alcohol pads at $6.90 each. The supplies are 20% off, and a $12.45 shipping charge is added after the discount. What is the total cost? Enter dollars to the nearest cent.

tr.175.2: Added the shipping without applying the discount.
tr.140.16: Applied the 20% discount to the shipping charge as well.

MA.q: A medical assistant counts 23 heartbeats in 20 seconds. At this rate, what is the patient's heart rate in beats per minute? Enter the number of beats per minute.

tr.46: Doubled the 20-second count instead of tripling it.
tr.1.15: Divided 23 by 20 to get beats per second and stopped.

MA.w: One minute is 60 seconds, which is 3 × 20 seconds. Heart rate = 23 × 3 = 69 beats per minute.

MA.q: A nurse's checklist has 5/6 of its tasks done. Which fraction with a denominator of 42 is equivalent to 5/6?
MA.w: 42 ÷ 6 = 7, so the denominator was multiplied by 7. Multiply the numerator by the same number: 5 × 7 = 35, giving 35/42. Check: 35/42 simplifies by 7 to 5/6.

n.0: 12/42 adds the factor 7 to the numerator (5 + 7) instead of multiplying by it.
n.1: 41/42 adds 36 to both the numerator and the denominator; adding changes the value.
n.2: 30/42 multiplies the numerator by 6, the old denominator, instead of by 7.

MA.q: Pharmacy A fills 135 prescriptions in 9 hours. Pharmacy B fills 48 prescriptions in 2 hours 40 minutes. How many more prescriptions per hour does Pharmacy B fill than Pharmacy A?
MA.w: Pharmacy A: 135 ÷ 9 = 15 per hour. Pharmacy B: 2 hours 40 minutes = 2 2/3 hours = 160 minutes; 48 ÷ 160 = 0.3 per minute × 60 = 18 per hour. Difference: 18 - 15 = 3.

n.1: This reads 2 hours 40 minutes as 2.4 hours, giving 48 ÷ 2.4 = 20 per hour for Pharmacy B.
n.2: This is Pharmacy B's rate, not the difference between the two rates.
n.3: This is Pharmacy A's rate, not the difference between the two rates.

MA.q: Tyrese buys nursing shoes and a watch for a combined $248 before tax. The sales tax rate is 7.25%. What is his total cost including tax? Enter the amount in dollars, to the nearest cent.

tr.17.98: Found the tax alone instead of the total cost.

MA.q: Dana earns $2,400 per month after taxes. Each month she pays $960 in rent, spends 1/6 of her after-tax income on food and puts $300 into savings. How much money does she have left each month?

n.0: $1,140 leaves out the food spending.
n.2: $1,040 leaves out the $300 put into savings.
n.3: $900 takes 1/6 of the money left after rent ($240) instead of 1/6 of her income.

MA.q: A patient is to receive 0.6 mg of a medication per day, divided into 2 equal doses. Tablets contain 0.15 mg each. How many tablets are given per dose?
MA.w: Each dose: 0.6 ÷ 2 = 0.3 mg. Desired ÷ have × quantity: 0.3 ÷ 0.15 × 1 = 2 tablets.

n.0: This is the number of tablets for the whole day (0.6 ÷ 0.15). The day's amount is split into 2 doses.
n.1: This is a decimal slip, dividing 0.3 by 0.015. Each tablet is 0.15 mg.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 0.15 ÷ 0.3 = 0.5. Divide the desired dose by the dose on hand.

MA.q: A nursing student records four lab values as 5/8, 0.6, 7/12 and 0.62. Which list is in order from least to greatest?

n.0: This places 5/8 before 0.62 as if 5/8 were less than 0.62; 5/8 = 0.625, which is greater than 0.62.
n.2: This places 7/12 after 0.62 as if its larger numerator made it larger; 7/12 = 0.583..., the least value.
n.3: This is greatest to least (descending), the reverse of the order asked.

MA.q: A hallway is 42 yards long. Baseboard trim is sold in 8-foot pieces. How many pieces must be bought to run trim along both long sides of the hallway? Assume there are no doorways.
MA.w: 42 yd × 3 = 126 ft per side, so both sides = 252 ft. 252 ÷ 8 = 31.5, so round up to 32 pieces.

n.0: 252 ÷ 8 = 31.5, and 31 pieces fall 4 feet short, so round up.
n.1: This does not convert yards to feet (84 ÷ 8 = 10.5, so 11); 1 yd = 3 ft.
n.2: This covers one side (126 ÷ 8 = 15.75, so 16); trim is needed on both sides.

MA.q: A toddler weighs 13.5 kg at a well-child visit. What is the toddler's weight in pounds, to the nearest tenth?
MA.w: Kilograms to pounds: multiply by 2.2. 13.5 × 2.2 = 29.7 lb. Check: 29.7 ÷ 2.2 = 13.5 kg.

n.1: This multiplies by 2 instead of 2.2.
n.2: This multiplies by 2.54, the inches-to-centimeters factor.
n.3: This divides by 2.2 (13.5 ÷ 2.2 = 6.1); kilograms to pounds means multiplying.

MA.q: What is IX × VI, written as a Roman numeral?
MA.w: IX = 9 and VI = 6. 9 × 6 = 54 = L + IV = LIV.

n.0: LVI = 50 + 5 + 1 = 56; 4 is written IV, with the I before the V, so 54 is LIV.
n.1: This reads VI as 4 (9 × 4 = 36); VI = 5 + 1 = 6.
n.2: This reads IX as 11 (11 × 6 = 66); I before X is subtracted, so IX = 9.

MA.q: A lab reports a sample concentration as the decimal 0.008. Which percent is equal to 0.008?
MA.w: Decimal to percent: multiply by 100 (move the point 2 places right). 0.008 × 100 = 0.8, so 0.8%.

n.0: 0.08% moves the decimal point only 1 place right.
n.1: 80% moves the decimal point 4 places right; 80% = 0.8.
n.2: 8% moves the decimal point 3 places right; 8% = 0.08.

MA.q: A vial contains 5 mL of medication. A nurse withdraws 1.25 mL for one patient and then 0.8 mL for a second patient. How much medication is left in the vial?
MA.w: Line up the decimal points. Amount withdrawn: 1.25 + 0.80 = 2.05 mL. Amount left: 5.00 - 2.05 = 2.95 mL.

n.0: 3.75 mL subtracts only the first withdrawal.
n.1: 3.67 mL treats 0.8 as 0.08 (lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points), so only 1.33 mL is subtracted.
n.3: 2.05 mL is the total withdrawn, not the amount left.

MA.q: An order is for 0.0375 g of a medication. Scored tablets contain 25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
MA.w: Convert: 0.0375 g × 1,000 = 37.5 mg. Desired ÷ have: 37.5 ÷ 25 = 1.5 tablets.

n.0: This converts 0.0375 g to 375 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 0.0375 g = 37.5 mg.
n.1: This converts 0.0375 g to 3.75 mg, moving the decimal point only two places.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 25 ÷ 37.5 = 0.67.

MA.q: Evaluate -4² + (-2)³.
MA.w: In -4² the exponent applies only to 4: -(4 × 4) = -16. In (-2)³ the parentheses include the sign: (-2)(-2)(-2) = -8. Sum: -16 + (-8) = -24.

n.0: 8 treats -4² as (-4)² = 16, then adds -8.
n.1: -8 treats (-2)³ as +8 (an odd number of negative factors is negative), giving -16 + 8.
n.2: -22 treats (-2)³ as -2 × 3 = -6; the exponent means multiplying -2 by itself three times.

MA.q: A county's sales tax rate is stored in a spreadsheet as the decimal 0.0375. What is this tax rate written as a percent? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.375: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.37.5: Moved the decimal point 3 places right.

MA.w: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.0375 × 100 = 3.75, so the rate is 3.75%.

MA.q: Marisol pays $378 per month for her car loan, which is 14% of her monthly take-home pay. What is her monthly take-home pay?

n.0: This multiplies 378 by 14 instead of dividing by 0.14.
n.1: This subtracts the $378 payment from $2,700, giving the pay left after the loan. The question asks for the whole take-home pay, of which $378 is 14%.
n.3: This treats 14% as 1/7 and multiplies 378 by 7. One-seventh is about 14.29%, not 14%, so the estimate is $54 too low.

MA.q: What is the value of the Roman numeral MCDXC?

n.0: This reads XC as 110 instead of 100 - 10 = 90.
n.2: This reads both pairs as sums (CD = 600, XC = 110).
n.3: This reads CD as 600 instead of 500 - 100 = 400.

MA.q: Darius's checking account was overdrawn, with a balance of -$37. He deposited $300 and then paid two bills of $84.50 and $128.50. What is his balance now? Enter the amount in whole dollars.

tr.124: Treated the starting balance as +$37 instead of -$37.
tr.263: Stopped after the deposit and did not subtract the two bills.

MA.q: An autoclave sterilizes instruments at 121 °C. What is this temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This adds 32 before multiplying ((121 + 32) × 1.8 = 275.4).
n.2: This uses the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula ((121 - 32) × 5/9 = 49.4).
n.3: This multiplies by 9/5 but leaves out adding 32.

MA.q: A hiker starts at a point 135 feet below sea level. She climbs 420 feet and then descends 190 feet. Where does she end up relative to sea level?
MA.w: Write the start as -135. Then -135 + 420 - 190 = 285 - 190 = 95. A positive result is above sea level: 95 ft above.

n.0: 365 treats the starting point as +135 instead of -135.
n.1: 475 adds the 190-foot descent instead of subtracting it.
n.3: The result, +95, is positive, so she is above sea level.

AP.q: A student is labeling a diagram of the male reproductive system. Which location should she label as the site where spermatogenesis, the production of sperm, takes place?
AP.w: Sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, supported by Sertoli cells. They then move to the epididymis to mature and be stored.

n.0: The ductus deferens carries sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct; it does not produce them.
n.1: The interstitial tissue between the tubules holds the Leydig cells, which make testosterone, not sperm.
n.2: The epididymis is where sperm mature and are stored after they are made, not where they are produced.

AP.q: When blood pressure and blood volume fall, the adrenal cortex increases its secretion of aldosterone. Which effect of aldosterone on the kidneys helps restore blood volume?
o: Reabsorbing Na⁺ (water follows) and excreting K⁺
Reabsorbing K⁺ (water follows) and excreting Na⁺
Excreting Na⁺ and water to reduce the workload on the heart
Reabsorbing Ca²⁺ in the distal tubule to raise blood volume
AP.w: Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb Na⁺, with water following by osmosis, and excrete K⁺. The retained water raises blood volume and blood pressure.

n.1: This reverses the ions: aldosterone causes Na⁺ retention and K⁺ excretion.
n.2: Excreting Na⁺ and water lowers blood volume; that is the action of ANP from the heart.
n.3: Increasing Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule is an action of PTH and controls blood calcium, not blood volume.

AP.q: A patient education leaflet groups the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra together because they work as a unit to remove wastes in urine. Which level of organization does this grouping represent?
o: Tissue, because the structures are lined by similar epithelial cells
Organ, because each structure contains two or more tissue types
Organ system, because several organs cooperate in one function
Organism, because removing wastes keeps the whole body alive
AP.w: Each structure listed is an organ. A group of organs that cooperate to carry out one major function is an organ system, here the urinary system.

n.0: A shared epithelial lining is one tissue within each organ. The leaflet groups whole organs, not a tissue.
n.1: That reasoning describes each structure on its own. The question asks about the group, and a group of cooperating organs is an organ system.
n.3: The organism level is the whole person made of all organ systems together, not a single system.

AP.q: In a healthy adult, how is most of the oxygen in arterial blood carried to the tissues?
o: Bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells
Bound to albumin and other plasma proteins
As bicarbonate ions carried in the plasma
Dissolved directly in the plasma around the cells
AP.w: About 98.5% of oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin; only about 1.5% is dissolved in plasma.

n.1: Albumin maintains osmotic pressure and carries some drugs and hormones; it is not an oxygen carrier.
n.2: Bicarbonate is the main carrier form of carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
n.3: Oxygen dissolves poorly in plasma, so only about 1.5% is carried this way.

AP.q: Which gland and hormone promote the maturation of T lymphocytes?
AP.w: The thymus, in the mediastinum behind the sternum, secretes thymosin, which promotes the maturation of T cells. The thymus is largest in childhood.

n.0: The thyroid secretes T3 and T4, which raise metabolic rate; the similar name is the trap.
n.1: Calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood calcium; it has no role in T-cell maturation.
n.2: The gland is right, but thyroxine comes from the thyroid; the thymus secretes thymosin.

AP.q: A new keratinocyte formed in the stratum basale is pushed toward the skin surface. Which epidermal layer does it enter next?
AP.w: Epidermal layers from deep to superficial: stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only) and corneum. A cell leaving the basale enters the stratum spinosum first.

n.0: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer of dead cells, the last layer the cell reaches.
n.2: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin and lies just below the corneum, far from the basale.
n.3: The stratum granulosum lies above the spinosum, so the cell reaches it later.

AP.q: The mediastinum is the central region of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs. Which structure is found in the mediastinum?
AP.w: The mediastinum contains the heart within its pericardial cavity, the trachea, the esophagus, the thymus and the great vessels.

n.0: The spinal cord is in the vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity, not the ventral thoracic cavity.
n.1: Each lung lies in its own pleural cavity on either side of the mediastinum.
n.3: The pleural cavities flank the mediastinum; they surround the lungs.

AP.q: A client's heart rate rises from 70 to 90 beats per minute while stroke volume falls from 80 mL to 70 mL per beat. What happens to cardiac output?
o: It stays at 5.6 L/min, as the changes offset
AP.w: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Before: 70 × 80 mL = 5,600 mL/min (5.6 L/min). After: 90 × 70 mL = 6,300 mL/min (6.3 L/min). Output rises.

n.0: 7.2 L/min is 90 × 80 mL: it applies the new heart rate but keeps the old stroke volume of 80 mL.
n.1: Cardiac output is a product, not a sum: the rise in rate (× 90/70) outweighs the fall in stroke volume (× 70/80).
n.2: 4.9 L/min is 70 × 70 mL: it applies the new stroke volume but keeps the old heart rate of 70.

AP.q: Blood pH starts to fall. Which defense acts within seconds, and which defense is the slowest but most powerful?
o: The kidneys act in seconds; the lungs are slowest
The lungs act in seconds; buffers are slowest
Buffers act in seconds; the kidneys are slowest
Buffers act in seconds; the lungs are slowest
AP.w: Chemical buffers such as the bicarbonate-carbonic acid system bind added H⁺ almost at once. The lungs adjust CO2 within minutes. The kidneys take hours to days but are the most powerful, secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing or making bicarbonate.

n.0: The kidneys are the slowest defense, taking hours to days, not seconds.
n.1: The lungs need minutes to change CO2, and buffers are the fastest defense, not the slowest.
n.3: Buffers are the fastest, but the lungs act within minutes; the kidneys are the slowest defense.

AP.q: Which sweat glands are distributed over most of the body surface, open directly onto the skin through pores, and secrete watery sweat that cools the body?
AP.w: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands are the most numerous, are found almost everywhere (especially palms, soles and forehead), open onto the surface through pores and secrete watery sweat for thermoregulation.

n.0: Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, usually into hair follicles; they do not produce sweat.
n.2: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands in the ear canal that produce earwax.
n.3: Apocrine glands are found in the axillary and anogenital regions, open into hair follicles and become active at puberty.

AP.q: The lining of the urinary bladder must stretch as the bladder fills and then return to its resting shape as it empties. Which tissue lines the bladder?
AP.w: Transitional epithelium is a stretchable epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ fills and empties. It lines the urinary bladder.

n.1: Stratified squamous epithelium is layered and protective (as in the epidermis) but is not the stretchable bladder lining.
n.2: Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells, as in the lining of the GI tract; it does not stretch like the bladder lining.
n.3: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments; it is not a lining tissue.

AP.q: Why does the electrical impulse pause briefly at the atrioventricular (AV) node before passing to the ventricles?
o: To let the atria refill with blood before they contract again
To let the SA node reset before it fires the next impulse
To let the semilunar valves close before the atria contract
To let the ventricles fill with blood before they contract
AP.w: The AV node delay gives the atria time to finish contracting and push blood into the ventricles, so the ventricles are full before they contract.

n.0: The atria refill during ventricular systole and diastole; the AV delay serves ventricular filling.
n.1: The SA node's timing does not depend on the AV node delay; the delay is about ventricular filling.
n.2: The semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular systole, not before atrial contraction.

AP.q: Which pairing of an accessory digestive organ with something it secretes into the digestive tract is correct?
AP.w: The exocrine pancreas releases pancreatic juice containing bicarbonate (to neutralize acid chyme) and enzymes such as lipase, amylase, trypsinogen and nucleases.

n.0: Pepsinogen is made by chief cells in the stomach; saliva contains amylase and lingual lipase.
n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, but the liver produces it.
n.3: Trypsin and chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes; the liver makes bile, not digestive enzymes.

AP.q: Bone is constantly remodeled. Based on the word parts, which bone cell breaks down bone matrix and releases calcium into the blood?
AP.w: oste/o means bone and -clast means breaker, so osteoclasts break down (resorb) bone matrix, releasing calcium.

n.1: chondr/o means cartilage: chondroblasts build cartilage matrix.
n.2: -cyte means cell: osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix around them.
n.3: -blast means builder: osteoblasts lay down new bone matrix.

AP.q: At rest, the inside of a typical neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside. Which mechanism uses ATP directly to help maintain this resting membrane potential?
o: Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels letting Na⁺ flow in
Ca²⁺ channels letting Ca²⁺ into the axon terminal
Na⁺/K⁺ pump moving 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in
AP.w: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in. Together with K⁺ leak channels, this keeps the inside of the resting neuron negative.

n.1: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold and cause depolarization; they are passive channels, not an ATP-driven pump.
n.2: Ca²⁺ channels at the axon terminal open during synaptic transmission; they do not maintain the resting potential.
n.3: The ratio is reversed: the pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

AP.q: How are the sutures that join the cranial bones of an adult skull classified, both by structure and by the amount of movement they allow?
o: Cartilaginous joints that are slightly movable
Fibrous joints that are slightly movable
AP.w: Sutures are fibrous joints: the bones are held together by short connective tissue fibers with no joint cavity. Functionally they are synarthroses (immovable).

n.0: Slightly movable cartilaginous joints (symphyses) include the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs.
n.1: Immovable cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) include the epiphyseal plate and the first rib-sternum joint, not sutures.
n.2: A slightly movable fibrous joint is a syndesmosis, such as the distal tibiofibular joint; sutures are immovable.

AP.q: A patient slowly lowers a dumbbell from shoulder height to the thigh, keeping the elbow under control. What type of contraction is the biceps brachii performing?
AP.w: Isotonic contractions change muscle length: concentric contractions shorten the muscle (curling the weight up) and eccentric contractions lengthen it while it stays under tension (lowering the weight slowly). Isometric contractions build tension with no change in length.

n.0: The biceps is not relaxed here: it stays under tension to control the descent, or the weight would simply drop.
n.1: A concentric contraction shortens the muscle, as when the dumbbell is curled up toward the shoulder.
n.3: An isometric contraction builds tension with no change in length, as when the dumbbell is held still.

AP.q: Several weeks after a kidney transplant, the recipient's immune system begins attacking the donor organ. Which cells directly kill the transplanted kidney cells?
AP.w: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells of cell-mediated immunity directly kill virus-infected cells, cancer cells and transplanted cells.

n.0: Helper T cells coordinate the attack through cytokines but do not kill the cells themselves.
n.1: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they do not make direct cell-to-cell kills.
n.3: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses; they would dampen rejection rather than carry it out.

AP.q: The wall of the urinary bladder must stretch a great deal as it fills with urine. Which tissue lines the bladder and allows this stretching?
AP.w: The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), whose cells change shape from rounded to flattened as the bladder fills.

n.0: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the digestive tract and is built for secretion and absorption.
n.1: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin layer built for diffusion and filtration, not for stretching.
n.2: Stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion, as in the skin and esophagus, but does not stretch like urothelium.

AP.q: A toxin blocks acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Which effect on the skeletal muscle fiber is expected?
o: ACh stays in the cleft and keeps stimulating the fiber
ACh release stops, so the fiber cannot be stimulated
Myosin heads cannot detach, as in rigor mortis
Ca²⁺ cannot leave the sarcoplasmic reticulum
AP.w: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft so the fiber can relax. If the enzyme is blocked, ACh lingers and keeps binding its receptors, so the fiber is stimulated again and again.

n.1: The enzyme breaks ACh down after release; blocking it does not stop the motor neuron from releasing ACh.
n.2: Myosin fails to detach when ATP runs out, as after death; this toxin affects ACh breakdown, not ATP supply.
n.3: Calcium release follows the muscle action potential, which lingering ACh makes more likely, not less.

AP.q: Which statement correctly describes the position of the heart in the thorax?
o: It lies in the left pleural cavity with its apex pointing up and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing down and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its base resting downward on the diaphragm
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing up and to the right
AP.w: The heart sits in the mediastinum between the lungs, enclosed in the pericardial cavity, with its apex pointing down, forward and to the left.

n.0: The pleural cavities surround the lungs; the heart is in the mediastinum, and its apex points down.
n.2: The broad base faces up and back toward the great vessels; the apex is the part that points down.
n.3: The apex points down and to the left, not up and to the right.

AP.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and the other is not. Why does an impulse travel faster along the myelinated axon?
o: Myelin carries the impulse in place of the axon membrane
The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
Myelin increases the size of each action potential
Myelin releases neurotransmitter along the axon's length
AP.w: Myelin insulates the axon, so the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier (gap in the myelin) to the next. This saltatory conduction is faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon.

n.0: Myelin is insulation; the action potential is still generated by the axon membrane at the nodes of Ranvier.
n.2: Action potentials are all-or-none; myelin speeds conduction but does not make each action potential larger.
n.3: Neurotransmitter is released from axon terminals at the synapse, not by myelin along the axon.

AP.q: A 64-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis several years after menopause. Which change in bone remodeling best accounts for her loss of bone mass?
o: Calcitonin rises and stimulates osteoclast resorption
Osteoblasts resorb more matrix as estrogen declines
AP.w: Bone is constantly remodeled by osteoblasts (which build) and osteoclasts (which resorb). After menopause estrogen falls, resorption exceeds formation, and bone mass is lost: osteoporosis.

n.0: If formation outpaced resorption, bone mass would increase rather than decrease.
n.2: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; it does not stimulate bone resorption.
n.3: Osteoblasts build bone; resorbing matrix is the job of osteoclasts.

AP.q: A surgeon reattaches a torn tendon to the outer surface of a long bone. Which structure covers that surface, carries blood vessels and nerves, and adds bone to increase the bone's width?
AP.w: The periosteum is the outer membrane of a bone: it carries vessels and nerves, anchors tendons, and adds bone to the surface (appositional growth in width) and during repair.

n.0: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces, is avascular and does not anchor tendons or add width.
n.1: The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavity, not the outer surface where tendons attach.
n.3: The synovial membrane lines a joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid; tendons do not anchor to it.

AP.q: Alcohol inhibits the secretion of ADH. Compared with a well-hydrated person who has not been drinking, what would be expected in a person who has had several alcoholic drinks?
o: Less water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more dilute urine
Less water reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so less urine
More water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so less urine
More Na⁺ reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more concentrated urine
AP.w: Two steps: ADH acts on the collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption, so less ADH means less water is reabsorbed there and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced.

n.1: ADH acts on the collecting ducts, not the proximal tubule, and reabsorbing less water produces more urine, not less.
n.2: This is the effect of more ADH; alcohol lowers ADH.
n.3: Na⁺ reabsorption is controlled by aldosterone, and lower ADH makes urine more dilute, not more concentrated.

AP.q: After a large meal, blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and blood glucose falls back to normal. Why is this classified as negative feedback?
o: The response lowers a variable, and any decrease counts as negative feedback
The response amplifies the rise until all of the glucose has been stored
The control center is a gland rather than the brain, which defines negative feedback
The response reverses the original change, bringing glucose back toward normal
AP.w: Negative feedback means the response opposes (reverses) the original change. A rise in glucose leads to a response that lowers it back toward the set point.

n.0: "Negative" refers to opposing the change, not to lowering a value. Releasing glucagon to raise low blood glucose is also negative feedback.
n.1: Amplifying a change describes positive feedback. Insulin opposes the rise in glucose.
n.2: Feedback type depends on whether the response opposes or amplifies the change, not on which structure acts as the control center.

AP.q: Shortly after a meal high in fat, cells of the duodenum release a hormone that makes the gallbladder contract. Which hormone is this, and what other effect does it have?
o: Secretin; it also triggers pancreatic bicarbonate release
Glucagon; it also triggers glycogen breakdown
Gastrin; it also triggers gastric acid secretion
Cholecystokinin; it also triggers pancreatic enzyme release
AP.w: Cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum makes the gallbladder contract to release bile and stimulates the pancreas to release its digestive enzymes.

n.0: Secretin does trigger bicarbonate release from the pancreas, but it is not the hormone that contracts the gallbladder.
n.1: Glucagon is a pancreatic islet hormone that raises blood glucose; it is not a duodenal hormone.
n.2: Gastrin comes from the stomach and stimulates acid secretion; it does not contract the gallbladder.

AP.q: A post-surgical note states that a patient's incision lies caudal to the umbilicus, on the patient's right side. Which organ lies in the same abdominal quadrant as the incision?
AP.w: Caudal is a synonym of inferior (toward the feet), so the incision is below the navel on the patient's right: the right lower quadrant, which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant. Choosing it treats caudal as if it meant cranial (toward the head).
n.2: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, which is cranial to the navel and on the patient's left.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is below the navel but in the left lower quadrant, on the patient's left side.

AP.q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels in a neuron while Na⁺ channels continue to work normally. Which phase of the action potential would be most directly impaired?
o: Ca²⁺ entry at the axon terminal
AP.w: Two steps: depolarization depends on Na⁺ entering through Na⁺ channels, while repolarization depends on K⁺ leaving through voltage-gated K⁺ channels. Blocking the K⁺ channels therefore impairs repolarization.

n.1: Depolarization is caused by Na⁺ entering through Na⁺ channels, which still work normally.
n.2: Ca²⁺ enters the axon terminal through Ca²⁺ channels, not K⁺ channels.
n.3: Threshold is reached as the stimulus opens Na⁺ channels; it does not depend on voltage-gated K⁺ channels.

AP.q: A patient sedated after surgery breathes slowly and shallowly for over an hour. Which change in the patient's arterial blood is expected?
o: CO₂ falls and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO₂ rises and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO₂ falls and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
CO₂ rises and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
AP.w: Step 1: hypoventilation removes too little CO₂, so CO₂ builds up. Step 2: CO₂ + H₂O forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, so pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

n.0: Falling CO₂ and rising pH follow hyperventilation, not slow shallow breathing.
n.1: CO₂ does rise, but extra CO₂ adds H⁺, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
n.2: Slow breathing retains CO₂, so CO₂ rises rather than falls.

BI.q: Two glucose molecules are joined to form the disaccharide maltose. Which description of this reaction is correct?
o: A water molecule is released, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is released, forming a glycosidic bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a glycosidic bond.
BI.w: Monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis, which releases water. Bonds between sugars are glycosidic bonds.

n.0: Peptide bonds join amino acids, not sugars.
n.2: This combines both errors: adding water breaks bonds, and peptide bonds join amino acids.
n.3: Adding water is hydrolysis, which breaks polymers apart rather than joining them.

BI.q: Hemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Why is the disorder seen much more often in males than in females?
o: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is expressed.
Males inherit the allele from their fathers.
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome.
The allele acts as dominant in males and recessive in females.
BI.w: Males (XY) have only one X chromosome (hemizygous), so a single recessive allele on it is expressed. Females need two copies to be affected.

n.1: Sons get their X from their mother; the father gives sons his Y.
n.2: The gene is on the X chromosome. Y-linked traits pass only from father to son.
n.3: The allele is recessive in both sexes; males show it because they have no second X to mask it.

BI.q: Glucose enters a muscle cell through GLUT carrier proteins, moving from higher concentration in the blood to lower concentration in the cell without using ATP. Which process is this?
BI.w: Movement down a concentration gradient through a carrier or channel protein, without ATP, is facilitated diffusion.

n.1: Active transport uses ATP and moves substances from low to high concentration. A carrier protein alone does not make transport active.
n.2: Simple diffusion passes straight through the bilayer with no protein. Glucose is too large and polar to do that.
n.3: Pinocytosis takes in droplets of fluid by vesicle and uses ATP; it is not carrier-mediated transport of single molecules.

BI.q: A heavy-metal ion binds to an enzyme away from its active site and changes the enzyme's shape. Adding more substrate does not restore activity. What is this?
BI.w: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes its shape, so extra substrate cannot overcome it.

n.0: Feedback inhibition is a pathway's end product slowing an early enzyme, not a heavy-metal ion.
n.1: Saturation is the plateau when all active sites are full; it is not inhibition.
n.2: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site, and more substrate can outcompete it.

BI.q: A pond freezes at the surface while fish survive in the water below. Why does ice float on liquid water?
o: Ice traps more dissolved air, which makes it lighter.
Freezing breaks hydrogen bonds and spreads molecules out.
Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open, less dense lattice.
Ice is denser but held up by surface tension.
BI.w: As water freezes, each molecule hydrogen-bonds to its neighbors in a rigid, open lattice. The molecules are farther apart than in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats.

n.0: Low density comes from the hydrogen-bonded lattice, not from trapped air.
n.1: Freezing forms stable hydrogen bonds; it does not break them.
n.3: Ice is less dense than liquid water; surface tension could not hold up a sheet of ice.

BI.q: Pepsin works in the stomach at about pH 2. If pepsin passes into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, what will most likely happen to its activity?
o: It will rise, since trypsin activates pepsin at pH 8.
It will stay the same, since a catalyst is not used up.
It will fall, since pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum.
It will rise, since enzymes work faster in basic solutions.
BI.w: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so at pH 8 its shape changes and activity falls. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, works in the small intestine.

n.0: Trypsin is a separate protein-digesting enzyme with its own optimum; it does not boost pepsin.
n.1: Catalysts are not consumed, but that does not protect pepsin's shape: at pH 8, far from its optimum, the enzyme loses activity.
n.3: Enzymes do not all work faster in basic conditions; each has its own optimum, and pepsin's is acidic.

BI.q: A biology tutor writes four statements on the board comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Which of the statements is accurate?
o: Prokaryotes divide by mitosis and eukaryotes by binary fission.
Prokaryotic DNA is linear and eukaryotic DNA is one circular loop.
Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and plants have cellulose walls.
Prokaryotic cells are usually larger than eukaryotic cells.
BI.w: Bacteria (prokaryotes) build their cell walls from peptidoglycan, and plants (eukaryotes) build theirs from cellulose. Each of the other statements reverses a real difference: cell size, method of division and form of the DNA.

n.0: This reverses the methods: prokaryotes divide by binary fission and eukaryotes use mitosis or meiosis.
n.1: This reverses the DNA forms: prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome and eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes.
n.3: This reverses the sizes: prokaryotic cells are smaller than eukaryotic cells.

BI.q: Which molecules made by the light-dependent reactions supply the energy for the Calvin cycle?
BI.w: The light reactions in the thylakoids make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma spends them to fix CO2 into sugar.

n.1: NADH and FADH2 are electron carriers of cellular respiration.
n.2: CO2 and water are raw materials of photosynthesis, not energy carriers.
n.3: O2 is a by-product released to the air, and glucose is a product of the Calvin cycle.

BI.q: At night, a houseplant takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. Which process explains this exchange?
o: The Calvin cycle in the chloroplast stroma
BI.w: Plants carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria all the time, using O2 and releasing CO2. Without light, photosynthesis stops, so respiration's gas exchange shows.

n.1: Fermentation is anaerobic and uses no oxygen; the vacuole stores water and wastes.
n.2: Photosynthesis uses CO2 and releases O2, the reverse, and needs light.
n.3: The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 into sugar rather than releasing it.

BI.q: Hemoglobin is built from four polypeptide chains fitted together into one working molecule. Which level of protein structure describes this arrangement?
BI.w: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains in one protein, as in hemoglobin's four chains.

n.0: Tertiary structure is the 3-D folding of a single chain.
n.1: Secondary structure is local coiling and folding (alpha helix, beta sheet) held by hydrogen bonds.
n.2: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence of one chain.

BI.q: Through which leaf structures does carbon dioxide enter for photosynthesis?
BI.w: CO2 diffuses into the leaf, and O2 out, through stomata: pores controlled by guard cells.

n.0: Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.
n.1: Thylakoids host the light reactions inside the chloroplast; they are not openings to the air.
n.3: Xylem carries water up from the roots, not CO2 from the air.

BI.q: A neuron and a white blood cell from the same patient differ greatly in shape and function. Which statement best explains this difference?
o: Each cell type expresses a different set of genes.
Each cell type lost the genes that it does not use.
Each cell type arose from a different mutation.
Each cell type holds a different set of genes.
BI.w: All body cells descend from one zygote by mitosis and carry the same DNA. Cells differentiate by switching different genes on and off (gene regulation), so each type makes its own set of proteins.

n.1: Differentiated cells keep the full set of genes; genes they do not need are switched off, not deleted.
n.2: Differentiation is controlled gene expression, not mutation; mutations are rare copying errors.
n.3: Body cells of one person carry the same DNA; what differs is which genes are used.

BI.q: A patient receives intravenous fluid of 0.9% sodium chloride rather than sterile pure water. Which statement best explains this choice at the level of the red blood cells?
o: It is hypotonic, so water moves into dehydrated red cells.
It is isotonic, so red cells neither gain nor lose water overall.
