It supplies the sodium that red cells absorb by active transport.
It is hypertonic, so excess water is drawn out of the red cells.
BI.w: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic to human cells, so there is no net water movement and the red cells keep their shape. Pure water is hypotonic and would cause hemolysis.

n.0: 0.9% NaCl is isotonic, not hypotonic. Pure water is the hypotonic fluid that would make red cells swell and burst.
n.2: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves sodium out of cells, not in, and the choice of saline is about tonicity.
n.3: 0.9% NaCl is not hypertonic. A hypertonic fluid would make red cells shrink (crenation).

BI.q: Mushrooms were once grouped with plants. Which feature shows that fungi belong in a separate kingdom?
o: They absorb food and have walls of chitin.
They lack a nucleus and membrane organelles.
They make food and have walls of cellulose.
They ingest food and have no cell walls.
BI.w: Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb food from their surroundings, and their cell walls are made of chitin. Plants make their own food and have cellulose walls.

n.1: Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; lacking them describes prokaryotes.
n.2: Making food by photosynthesis and having cellulose walls describes plants, not fungi.
n.3: Ingesting food with no cell walls describes animals; fungi have chitin walls and absorb food.

BI.q: A cell copies its DNA during S phase. After one round of replication, what does each of the two new DNA double helices contain?
o: Original and new pieces mixed in each strand
Two newly made strands, with no old DNA
One original strand and one new strand
BI.w: DNA replication is semiconservative: each strand serves as a template, so every new double helix keeps one original strand and gains one new strand.

n.0: Mixed pieces within each strand would be dispersive replication, which was ruled out experimentally.
n.1: If both helices were entirely new, the original DNA would be lost; each helix keeps one parent strand.
n.2: Two original strands rejoined would be conservative replication, which is not how DNA copies.

BI.q: Very small and large eggs of one bird species hatch less often than medium eggs, so over generations egg size clusters near the middle. Which type of selection is this?
BI.w: Stabilizing selection favors the average and acts against both extremes, so the range narrows around the middle.

n.1: Directional selection favors one extreme, shifting the average one way.
n.2: Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the average, the reverse of this case.
n.3: Artificial selection is breeding chosen by humans; here survival in nature decides.

BI.q: Which bonds hold neighboring molecules together in liquid water?
o: Ionic bonds between H+ and OH- ions
BI.w: Hydrogen bonds form between the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule and the partially negative oxygen of a neighbor. They are weak one by one but strong together.

n.0: Polar covalent bonds join oxygen and hydrogen inside each molecule, not neighboring molecules.
n.1: Water ionizes only slightly; liquid water is held together by hydrogen bonds, not ionic bonds.
n.3: Oxygen atoms of neighboring molecules do not share electrons; the attraction is hydrogen bonding.

BI.q: A researcher sequences the stretch of chromosome 7 that holds the instructions for making the CFTR protein. Which term best describes this stretch of DNA?
BI.w: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein (or a functional RNA).

n.0: A codon is three bases that code for one amino acid; a whole protein needs many codons.
n.1: A genome is all of an organism's DNA, not one protein-coding segment.
n.2: Chromosome 7 is the whole DNA molecule; the CFTR instructions are one stretch of it.

BI.q: A bean seed has sat unchanged in a jar for two years. Which observation would best show that the seed is alive?
o: Its cells use energy and divide after watering.
It has a hard, protective outer coat.
It gains mass after soaking in water overnight.
It is built from carbon-containing molecules.
BI.w: Living things are made of cells that use energy (metabolism) and grow by cell division. A seed whose cells start respiring and dividing after watering is alive.

n.1: A hard coat protects the embryo, but nonliving objects such as shells and stones also have hard coverings.
n.2: Gaining mass by soaking up water is absorption; a dry sponge does the same without being alive.
n.3: Dead wood, paper and oil are also built from carbon compounds, so this does not show life.

BI.q: A slide shows cells with a rigid outer boundary, a large central vacuole and green, disk-shaped organelles. Which other structure would these cells also be expected to contain?
o: A nucleoid region instead of a nucleus
A cell wall made of peptidoglycan
BI.w: The wall, central vacuole and chloroplasts identify a plant cell. Plant cells carry out cellular respiration in mitochondria as well as photosynthesis in chloroplasts.

n.0: A nucleoid region is a prokaryotic feature. Plant cells are eukaryotic and have a membrane-bound nucleus.
n.1: Peptidoglycan walls belong to bacteria. A plant cell wall is made of cellulose.
n.2: Glycogen is the animal storage polysaccharide; plant cells store glucose as starch.

BI.q: A textbook describes the two strands of a DNA double helix as antiparallel. What does this term mean?
o: The two strands run in opposite directions.
One strand is made of DNA and the other of RNA.
The strands are joined by covalent bonds between bases.
The two strands carry the same base sequence.
BI.w: Antiparallel means the two strands run in opposite directions: one runs 5' to 3' and its partner runs 3' to 5'.

n.1: Both strands of the double helix are DNA. DNA-RNA pairing happens only briefly during transcription.
n.2: Bases are joined across the strands by hydrogen bonds; that describes bonding, not direction.
n.3: The strands are complementary (A-T, G-C), not identical in sequence.

BI.q: Before a newly made pre-mRNA leaves the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, it is processed. Which change occurs during this processing?
o: Introns are removed and exons are joined.
Codons are translated into amino acids.
Thymine bases are replaced by uracil.
Exons are removed and introns are joined.
BI.w: During processing, introns (noncoding regions) are cut out and exons (coding regions) are spliced together; a 5' cap and poly-A tail are also added.

n.1: Translation happens later, at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA leaves the nucleus.
n.2: RNA is built with uracil from the start; no thymine is present in pre-mRNA to replace.
n.3: This is reversed: introns are removed and exons are kept.

BI.q: During a sprint, a runner's leg muscle cells run short of oxygen. Which stage of glucose breakdown can continue to supply these cells with ATP?
o: The Krebs cycle in the matrix
BI.w: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen, netting 2 ATP per glucose. With lactic acid fermentation regenerating what glycolysis needs, it keeps running when oxygen is short.

n.0: The Krebs cycle depends on the electron transport chain, which needs oxygen, so it slows when oxygen runs short.
n.2: Pyruvate oxidation makes no ATP and stalls without oxygen, since the electron transport chain no longer regenerates NAD+.
n.3: The electron transport chain requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor, so it stops without oxygen.

BI.q: A student is reviewing how the three ABO alleles (IA, IB and i) interact. Which statement about the ABO blood group system is accurate?
o: IA is dominant over IB, so a person with IAIB is type A.
IA and IB blend by incomplete dominance into type AB.
The i allele is dominant, so one copy gives type O.
The i allele is recessive to both the IA and IB alleles.
BI.w: ABO shows multiple alleles: IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. Type O requires ii.

n.0: IA and IB are codominant; a person with IAIB expresses both and is type AB.
n.1: Type AB shows both A and B antigens fully, which is codominance, not a blend.
n.2: i is recessive. A person must have two copies (ii) to be type O.

BI.q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
BI.w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

BI.q: A karyotype is prepared from a body cell of a healthy human female. Which description of her chromosomes is accurate?
o: 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
23 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of X chromosomes
22 pairs of autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome
46 pairs of chromosomes, including two X chromosomes
BI.w: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes, XX in a female.

n.1: This adds up to 24 pairs (48 chromosomes). There are 22 pairs of autosomes, not 23.
n.2: An X and a Y is the male sex chromosome pair.
n.3: Humans have 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs, not 46 pairs.

BI.q: A breeder wants to know whether a black guinea pig is BB or Bb, where black (B) is dominant over white (b). Which cross would best answer this?
o: Cross it with a heterozygous black (Bb) guinea pig.
Cross it with a homozygous black (BB) guinea pig.
Cross it with another black guinea pig of unknown genotype.
Cross it with a white (bb) guinea pig.
BI.w: A test cross pairs the unknown dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive (bb). Any white offspring prove the unknown parent carries b, so it is Bb.

n.0: A Bb partner passes on b only half the time, so white pups appear less often (1/4 instead of 1/2 if the unknown is Bb). It is a weaker test than crossing with bb.
n.1: Every offspring of a BB parent shows black whatever the other parent is, so the cross cannot reveal a hidden b allele.
n.2: An unknown partner adds a second unknown, so the results cannot be interpreted.

BI.q: After years of heavy antibiotic use, most bacteria of one species in a hospital are resistant. Which explanation fits natural selection?
o: The antibiotic caused new resistance mutations in the cells.
Each bacterium developed resistance because it needed it.
Resistant bacteria already present survived and multiplied.
Bacteria exposed to the drug grew tougher and passed it on.
BI.w: Resistance alleles already existed in a few bacteria. The antibiotic killed the susceptible cells, the resistant ones survived and reproduced, and over generations the population became mostly resistant.

n.0: The antibiotic does not cause the mutation; it selects bacteria that already carried resistance.
n.1: Organisms do not develop traits because they need them; the variation must exist first.
n.3: Toughening during an organism's life is an acquired trait, and acquired traits are not inherited.

BI.q: Leaf cells of the pond plant Elodea are placed in concentrated salt water and viewed under a microscope. Which change is seen in the cells?
o: Water leaves, and the membrane pulls away from the wall.
Salt enters, and the swollen cells burst their walls.
Water leaves, and the cell walls shrivel and crenate.
Water enters, and the cells press firmly on their walls.
BI.w: Concentrated salt water is hypertonic to the cells, so water leaves by osmosis. The rigid cellulose wall keeps its shape while the membrane shrinks away from it: plasmolysis.

n.1: Osmosis moves water, not salt, and here the cells lose water; the wall also keeps plant cells from bursting.
n.2: Crenation is the shrinking of wall-less red blood cells. A plant cell wall is rigid and keeps its shape; the membrane pulls away from it instead.
n.3: Water entry and turgor follow a hypotonic solution such as pure water; concentrated salt water is hypertonic.

BI.q: A student compares mitosis and meiosis in a table. Which event occurs in meiosis but does not occur in mitosis?
o: Formation of a spindle from microtubules
BI.w: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and form tetrads only in prophase I of meiosis. The other events happen in both processes.

n.0: DNA is replicated once, during S phase, before both mitosis and meiosis.
n.2: Sister chromatids separate in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II of meiosis.
n.3: A microtubule spindle moves chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis.

CH.q: A homeowner notices four changes in the kitchen over one weekend. Which of these is a chemical change rather than a physical change?
o: Sugar dissolving and vanishing in a mug of hot tea
Bubbles forming throughout a pot of boiling water
A cut apple slice turning brown on the counter
Frost forming on the inside of the freezer door
CH.w: A cut apple browns because compounds in the fruit react with oxygen in the air to form new, brown substances: a chemical change signaled by a color change. Dissolving, boiling and deposition change form or state but leave the same substance.

n.0: Dissolving is physical: the sugar molecules are still sugar and can be recovered by evaporating the water, even though they seem to vanish.
n.1: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, still H₂O, so boiling is a physical change of state despite the gas.
n.3: Frost forms by deposition, water vapor turning directly into ice; a new solid appears, but it is still H₂O, so the change is physical.

CH.q: Burning natural gas on a stove and photosynthesis in a plant leaf are both chemical reactions. Which statement correctly classifies their energy changes?
o: Burning is exothermic; photosynthesis is endothermic
Both are endothermic, because both need energy to start
Both are exothermic, because both involve oxygen gas
Burning is endothermic; photosynthesis is exothermic
CH.w: Combustion releases heat and light to the surroundings (exothermic). Photosynthesis absorbs energy from sunlight and stores it in glucose (endothermic).

n.1: Needing a spark to start describes activation energy; a reaction that starts this way can still release more energy than it absorbs overall.
n.2: Involving oxygen does not decide the energy change; photosynthesis absorbs energy even though it releases oxygen.
n.3: This reverses the two. Burning warms the surroundings, while photosynthesis takes in light energy.

CH.q: What percentage of a radioactive sample has decayed after exactly 2 half-lives?
CH.w: After 1 half-life 50% remains; after 2 half-lives 25% remains. The part that has decayed is 100% − 25% = 75%.

n.1: 25% is the amount still remaining after 2 half-lives, not the amount that has decayed.
n.2: 87.5% has decayed after 3 half-lives (12.5% left), one half-life too many.
n.3: 50% has decayed after 1 half-life; the second half-life decays half of the remaining 50%.

CH.q: When a sample containing sodium is held in a flame, the flame turns a bright yellow-orange. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this colored light?
o: Electrons absorbing heat and moving to higher energy levels
Excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels
Protons leaving the nucleus as the atoms are strongly heated
Sodium atoms combining with oxygen to form a new compound
CH.w: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back to lower levels, they emit the extra energy as light of specific colors, which is why each element has a characteristic flame color and emission spectrum.

n.0: Absorbing energy raises electrons to higher levels, but light is given off when they drop back down, not as they move up.
n.2: Protons do not leave the nucleus in a flame; flame color comes from electron transitions.
n.3: Flame color is a property of the element's electrons, not of a combustion product; sodium compounds give the same color.

CH.q: A pharmacy technician sorts four samples on a shelf. Which of these samples is a homogeneous mixture?
CH.w: Salt water is a solution, a homogeneous mixture: the dissolved salt is spread evenly, so every part has the same composition, and the proportions can vary.

n.0: Oil and vinegar separate into visible layers, so the dressing is a heterogeneous mixture.
n.1: Distilled water is a pure substance, the compound H₂O, not a mixture.
n.2: Sand does not dissolve and settles out, so sand in water is a heterogeneous mixture (a suspension).

CH.q: Zinc is more active than copper. Which products form when a zinc strip is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution, CuSO₄?
CH.w: Single replacement: the more active zinc replaces copper. Zn²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ as ZnSO₄, and copper metal forms: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

n.0: Zn²⁺ balances one SO₄²⁻, so the formula is ZnSO₄, not Zn(SO₄)₂.
n.2: No reaction would occur with copper metal in a zinc salt; here the more active metal is the free element.
n.3: Zinc does not take oxygen from sulfate; it simply swaps places with copper.

CH.q: A particle has 20 protons, 22 neutrons and 18 electrons. Calcium has atomic number 20 and argon has atomic number 18. Which best identifies this particle?
o: A calcium-42 cation with a charge of 2+
A calcium-38 cation with a charge of 2+
A calcium-42 anion with a charge of 2-
An argon-40 atom with no net charge
CH.w: Step 1: 20 protons means the element is calcium, and the mass number is 20 + 22 = 42. Step 2: 20 positive charges and 18 negative charges give a net charge of 2+. The particle is a calcium-42 ion, Ca²⁺.

n.1: 38 adds protons and electrons. Mass number is protons plus neutrons: 20 + 22 = 42.
n.2: With two fewer electrons than protons, the charge is positive. A 2- ion would need 22 electrons.
n.3: The element is set by protons, not electrons. Having 18 electrons does not make it argon.

CH.q: A radioactive tracer has a half-life of 6 hours. A 40 mg dose is prepared at 8:00 a.m. How much of the tracer remains undecayed at 2:00 a.m. the next day?
CH.w: From 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. is 18 hours, which is 18 / 6 = 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount: 40 mg to 20 mg to 10 mg to 5 mg (1/8 of the original).

n.0: This divides 40 by 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount; it does not remove an equal share.
n.1: 2.5 mg would remain after 4 half-lives (24 hours), one half-life too many.
n.2: 10 mg remains after 2 half-lives (12 hours, at 8:00 p.m.), not after the full 18 hours.

CH.q: Phosphorus has atomic number 15 and sits in period 3, group 15 of the periodic table. How many valence electrons does a neutral phosphorus atom have?
CH.w: Phosphorus has 15 electrons arranged 2, 8, 5, so its outer shell holds 5 valence electrons. For main-group elements in groups 13-18, the valence count is the group number minus 10 (group 15 = 5).

n.1: 15 is the atomic number and the group number, but group 15 elements have 5 valence electrons, not 15.
n.2: 10 is the number of inner (core) electrons in the first two shells, not the outer-shell electrons.
n.3: 3 is the period number (the number of occupied shells), or the number of electrons phosphorus needs to complete an octet; neither is its valence count.

CH.q: What is the molar mass of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂? (Use Mg = 24.3, O = 16.0, H = 1.0.)
CH.w: The subscript 2 doubles everything in the parentheses: 24.3 + 2(16.0 + 1.0) = 24.3 + 34.0 = 58.3 g/mol.

n.0: 82.6 doubles the magnesium as well; only the OH group is doubled.
n.2: 42.3 doubles the hydrogen but not the oxygen; the 2 applies to the whole OH group.
n.3: 41.3 ignores the subscript 2 and counts only one OH group.

CH.q: On a reaction energy diagram, the curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to the products. What does the rise from the reactants to the peak represent?
o: The activation energy needed to start the reaction
The change in energy between reactants and products
The energy stored in the bonds of the products
The total energy released by the reaction
CH.w: The 'hill' between the reactants and the peak is the activation energy, the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. A catalyst lowers this peak.

n.1: The overall energy change (delta H) is the difference between the reactant and product levels, which does not include the peak.
n.2: The energy of the products is the level of the curve after the peak, not the height of the climb.
n.3: The energy released is the drop from the reactants down to the products, not the rise to the peak.

CH.q: A copper wire placed in silver nitrate solution becomes coated with silver: Cu + 2 AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2 Ag. What explains this reaction?
o: Copper is more active than silver, so copper replaces silver
Silver is more active than copper, so silver replaces copper
Nitrate ions trade places between two compounds in solution
Copper and silver combine to form a single new compound
CH.w: This is single replacement: a free metal replaces a less active metal in a compound. Copper is above silver in the activity series, so copper ions go into solution and silver metal comes out.

n.1: If silver were more active, no reaction would occur; the more active metal does the replacing.
n.2: Only one reactant is a compound; a free element replacing another is single, not double, replacement.
n.3: There are two products, Cu(NO₃)₂ and Ag, so this is not synthesis.

CH.q: An antacid containing magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, is taken to neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. What are the products of this neutralization reaction?
CH.w: Acid + base → salt + water. Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + 2 H₂O: the salt is magnesium chloride, and H⁺ from the acid joins OH⁻ from the base to form water.

n.0: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a hydroxide base.
n.1: Carbon dioxide forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate antacid (such as CaCO₃); magnesium hydroxide contains no carbon.
n.3: Neutralization swaps ions to give a salt and water; it does not produce chlorine gas or an oxide.

CH.q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. Which of these quantities identifies the atom as the element chlorine rather than some other element?
o: Its mass number of 35, the sum of its nucleons
Its 17 protons, which set its atomic number
Its 18 neutrons, which fix the mass of the isotope
Its 17 electrons, which balance the nuclear charge
CH.w: The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons, and it alone defines the element and its place on the periodic table. Every chlorine atom has 17 protons; any atom with 17 protons is chlorine.

n.0: The mass number (protons + neutrons) identifies a particular isotope, not the element; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are both chlorine.
n.2: Neutron number varies between isotopes of the same element, so it cannot identify the element.
n.3: Electron number can change when an atom becomes an ion (Cl⁻ has 18 electrons) without changing the element.

CH.q: Hydrogen peroxide stored in a clear bottle slowly breaks down when exposed to light, according to the equation 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. Which type of reaction is this?
CH.w: A decomposition reaction (AB → A + B) breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen.

n.1: Single replacement needs a free element replacing another in a compound; there is only one reactant here.
n.2: Combustion is a fuel reacting with O₂ to produce CO₂ and H₂O; here O₂ is produced, not consumed.
n.3: Synthesis is the reverse pattern: two or more reactants combine into one product.

CH.q: An unknown element is dull, brittle as a solid, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity. In which region of the periodic table is it most likely found?
o: The upper right, among the nonmetals
The left side, among the alkali metals
The center, among the transition metals
The staircase line, among the metalloids
CH.w: Dull luster, brittleness and poor conductivity are the properties of nonmetals, which are found in the upper right of the periodic table (plus hydrogen).

n.1: Alkali metals are shiny, soft metals that conduct heat and electricity well.
n.2: Transition metals are shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors.
n.3: Metalloids have intermediate properties and are semiconductors; they conduct better than typical nonmetals.

CH.q: Normal saline used for IV fluids is 0.9% (w/v) sodium chloride. How many grams of sodium chloride are dissolved in 1 liter of normal saline?
CH.w: Step 1: % (w/v) means grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, so 0.9% is 0.9 g per 100 mL. Step 2: 1 liter is 1,000 mL, or 10 x 100 mL, so the bag holds 0.9 x 10 = 9 g of NaCl.

n.0: 0.9 g is the amount in 100 mL, not in a full liter.
n.1: 0.09 g misplaces the decimal point; it is ten times too small even for 100 mL, let alone a liter.
n.3: 90 g would be a 9% solution; this moves the decimal point one place too far.

CH.q: Which coefficients, in order, balance C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O in lowest whole numbers?
CH.w: 2 C₂H₆ gives 4 C and 12 H, so 4 CO₂ and 6 H₂O. Oxygen on the right = 8 + 6 = 14 atoms = 7 O₂. Check: C 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 14 = 14.

n.0: 4, 14, 8, 12 is balanced but not in lowest whole numbers; divide by 2.
n.1: 1, 3, 2, 3 gives 6 O on the left but 7 on the right; ethane needs 3.5 O₂, so double everything.
n.3: With 2 C₂H₆ there are 12 H atoms, so 6 H₂O are needed, not 3.

CH.q: Magnesium, an element needed for muscle and nerve function, has atomic number 12. Which arrangement of electrons, listed by shell from the nucleus outward, describes a neutral magnesium atom?
CH.w: Electrons fill the lowest shells first. The first shell holds 2 and the second holds 8, which accounts for 10 electrons; the remaining 2 go into the third shell: 2, 8, 2. Magnesium therefore has 2 valence electrons, matching its place in group 2.

n.0: The second shell fills to 8 before any electrons enter the third shell.
n.1: The third shell can hold more than 1 electron, so both remaining electrons go into it rather than starting a fourth shell.
n.3: The second shell holds a maximum of 8 electrons, so it cannot hold 10.

CH.q: A sealed syringe holds 20 mL of air at 1 atm. At constant temperature, the plunger is pushed in until the pressure doubles. What is the new volume of the air?
CH.w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related (P1V1 = P2V2). 1 atm x 20 mL = 2 atm x V2, so V2 = 20 / 2 = 10 mL. Doubling the pressure halves the volume.

n.0: 5 mL would be the volume if the pressure were quadrupled, not doubled.
n.1: This treats pressure and volume as directly related. They are inversely related, so the volume falls.
n.2: Gases are compressible; the volume changes when the pressure changes.

CH.q: A chemistry teacher asks which pair of elements would most likely combine to form an ionic compound. Which pair should the students choose?
CH.w: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal with a large electronegativity difference. Potassium (an alkali metal) readily loses an electron to bromine (a halogen), forming KBr.

n.0: Copper and zinc are both metals; together they form an alloy (brass) held by metallic bonding.
n.2: Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals and form covalent bonds, as in PCl₃.
n.3: Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons in covalent bonds.

CH.q: A cook notices that olive oil forms a separate layer on water but dissolves easily in hexane, a liquid made of nonpolar molecules. Which statement explains this behavior?
o: Hexane is denser than water, so it holds more dissolved oil
Nonpolar oil dissolves in nonpolar hexane but not in polar water
Oil is an ionic compound that dissolves best in hexane
Polar oil dissolves in polar hexane but not in nonpolar water
CH.w: 'Like dissolves like': nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents, and polar or ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents. Oil is nonpolar, so it mixes with hexane but not with polar water.

n.0: Density decides which layer floats, not whether a substance dissolves; hexane is actually less dense than water.
n.2: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents such as water, not in nonpolar hexane; oil is nonpolar and molecular.
n.3: The rule is applied correctly, but the labels are reversed: oil and hexane are nonpolar, and water is polar.

CH.q: What is the percent by mass of carbon in carbon dioxide, CO₂? (Use C = 12.0, O = 16.0.)
CH.w: Molar mass of CO₂ = 44.0 g/mol, of which 12.0 g is carbon. 12.0 ÷ 44.0 × 100 = 27.3%.

n.0: 33.3% counts atoms (1 of 3) instead of mass.
n.2: 42.9% uses 28.0 g/mol, counting one oxygen instead of two.
n.3: 72.7% is the percent of oxygen, not carbon.

CH.q: A student tests four liquids with a simple conductivity tester that lights a bulb when current flows. Which liquid will light the bulb?
o: Ethanol mixed with an equal volume of water
CH.w: Ionic compounds such as KCl dissociate into ions (K⁺ and Cl⁻) in water. Mobile ions carry current, so the solution is an electrolyte and conducts electricity.

n.0: Sucrose dissolves as whole molecules, not ions, so its solution is a nonelectrolyte.
n.1: Pure water contains too few ions to conduct noticeably; dissolved ions are what make tap and salt water conduct.
n.2: Ethanol dissolves as neutral molecules, so the mixture does not conduct.

CH.q: A model of an atom is being built for a classroom display. Which statement correctly describes where most of an atom's mass and most of its volume are found?
o: Most mass is in the nucleus; most volume is the electron cloud
Most mass and most volume are both in the nucleus
Most mass is in the electron cloud; most volume is the nucleus
Mass is split evenly between the nucleus and the electron cloud
CH.w: Protons and neutrons (each about 1 amu) are in the nucleus, so the nucleus holds nearly all the mass. Electrons are nearly massless but occupy the electron cloud, which takes up nearly all of the atom's volume.

n.1: The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom; the electron cloud takes up almost all the volume.
n.2: This reverses the facts. Electrons have negligible mass, and the nucleus is a tiny fraction of the volume.
n.3: Electrons have about 1/1836 the mass of a proton, so the electron cloud contributes almost no mass.

CH.q: In the reaction 2 Al + 3 CuCl₂ → 2 AlCl₃ + 3 Cu, which element is reduced, and what is its reactant called?
o: Chlorine; CuCl₂ is the oxidizing agent
Copper; CuCl₂ is the reducing agent
Aluminum; Al is the oxidizing agent
Copper; CuCl₂ is the oxidizing agent
CH.w: Copper goes from +2 in CuCl₂ to 0 in Cu: it gains electrons and is reduced. The substance that is reduced is the oxidizing agent. Aluminum (0 to +3) is oxidized and is the reducing agent.

n.0: Chlorine stays at −1 on both sides, so it is neither oxidized nor reduced.
n.1: Copper is reduced, but the substance reduced is the oxidizing agent, not the reducing agent.
n.2: Aluminum loses electrons (0 to +3), so it is oxidized and acts as the reducing agent.

CH.q: Which pair of substances, dissolved together in water, would act as a buffer?
CH.w: A buffer is a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Carbonic acid (weak) and bicarbonate (its conjugate base) form the main buffer in blood.

n.1: HCl and Mg(OH)₂ neutralize each other to form a salt and water; they are not a weak acid and its conjugate base.
n.2: NaOH is a strong base and Na₂SO₄ a neutral salt; there is no weak acid to absorb added OH⁻.
n.3: HNO₃ is a strong acid; nitrate is too weak a base to absorb added H⁺, so this pair does not buffer.

CH.q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. Which statement about these hydrogen bonds is correct?
o: They are stronger than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when electrons transfer from hydrogen to nitrogen
They are weaker than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when hydrogen shares an electron pair with carbon
CH.w: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. They are much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why DNA strands can be separated for replication while each strand's backbone stays intact.

n.0: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds; that weakness lets the strands unzip.
n.1: Hydrogen bonds involve partial charges, not a transfer of electrons, which would make ions.
n.3: A C-H bond is an ordinary covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen attached to N, O or F.

CH.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
CH.w: In a polyatomic ion the oxidation numbers add up to the ion's charge: S + 4(−2) = −2, so S = +6.

n.1: +8 sets the sum to 0; the sum must equal the ion's charge, −2.
n.2: +2 uses −1 for each oxygen; oxygen is −2 here.
n.3: −2 is the charge of the whole ion (and of sulfide), not sulfur's oxidation number in sulfate.

CH.q: A student is classifying four compounds by bond type. Which of these compounds is held together by covalent bonds?
CH.w: Covalent bonds form when nonmetal atoms share electron pairs. Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so CO₂ is a covalent (molecular) compound.

n.1: Potassium is a metal, so potassium bromide is ionic (K⁺ and Br⁻).
n.2: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so MgO is ionic (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻).
n.3: Calcium is a metal, so calcium chloride is ionic (Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻).

PH.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at 35° measured from the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection measured from the normal?
PH.w: Angles are measured from the normal: 90° - 35° = 55° of incidence, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence: 55°.

n.1: 110° is the angle between the incident and reflected rays (55° + 55°), not the angle of reflection from the normal.
n.2: Doubles the surface angle; the law compares the incidence and reflection angles, both from the normal.
n.3: 35° is measured from the surface; the law of reflection uses the normal.

PH.q: In a vacuum, how does the speed of radio waves compare with the speed of X-rays?
o: Each speed is set by the wavelength
They travel at the same speed
PH.w: All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed.

n.0: Wavelength and frequency change together (c = f λ) while the speed stays c.
n.2: Higher frequency does not mean higher speed in a vacuum.
n.3: Longer wavelength does not mean higher speed in a vacuum.

PH.q: Two objects attract each other with gravitational force F. If one mass is doubled and the distance between their centers is halved, what is the new force?
PH.w: F is proportional to m1 m2 / r². Doubling one mass gives x2; halving r gives x(2²) = x4. Together: 2 x 4 = 8F.

n.1: Counts only the x4 from halving r and leaves out the x2 from doubling one mass.
n.2: Treats halving r as halving the force, cancelling the doubled mass.
n.3: Squares both changes; the mass factor is not squared.

PH.q: Why does a transformer work with alternating current but not with steady direct current?
o: Direct current demagnetizes the iron core
Alternating current makes a stronger steady field
Direct current cannot flow through copper coils
It needs a changing magnetic field to induce voltage
PH.w: A transformer works by induction: the changing current in one coil makes a changing field that induces voltage in the other. Steady DC makes a steady field, which induces nothing.

n.0: DC does not demagnetize the core; its unchanging field simply induces no voltage.
n.1: AC is useful here because its field changes, not because it is stronger.
n.2: DC flows through copper coils easily; the problem is that its field does not change.

PH.q: Why does a sharp needle pierce skin more easily than a blunt one pushed with the same force?
o: A larger area gives a greater pressure
A smaller area gives a greater force
A smaller area gives less friction
A smaller area gives a greater pressure
PH.w: P = F / A. With the same force, the needle's tiny tip area produces a much greater pressure.

n.0: A larger area spreads the force and lowers the pressure.
n.1: The force is the same for both needles; it is the pressure that rises.
n.2: Piercing depends on pressure at the tip, not on friction.

PH.q: A 9.0 V battery is connected across a 3.0 Ω resistor. What current flows? (V = IR)

n.0: Subtracts R from V; Ohm's law divides.
n.2: Multiplies V by R; Ohm's law gives I = V / R.
n.3: Inverts the formula (R / V).

PH.q: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
o: They point toward positive and away from negative charges
They point away from both positive and negative charges
They point away from positive and toward negative charges
They are spaced farther apart where the field is stronger
PH.w: Field lines show the direction of force on a positive test charge: away from positive charges, toward negative charges. Closer lines mean a stronger field.

n.0: Reverses the direction of the field lines.
n.1: A positive test charge is pulled toward a negative charge, so lines point into it.
n.3: Closer, not farther, spacing shows a stronger field.

PH.q: A velocity-time graph for a scooter shows a straight line rising from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 12 m/s at t = 6.0 s. How far does the scooter travel in those 6.0 s?
PH.w: Displacement = area under a v-t graph. The area is a triangle: 1/2 x 6.0 s x 12 m/s = 36 m.

n.0: Uses the full rectangle (6.0 x 12) and leaves out the 1/2 for a triangle.
n.2: Reads the final velocity off the graph instead of the area under it.
n.3: 2.0 is the slope (12 / 6.0 = 2.0 m/s²): the acceleration, not the distance.

PH.q: As a sound wave travels through air, how do the air molecules move?
o: Along with the wave from source to listener
In circles around the wave's direction
Up and down, perpendicular to the wave
Back and forth, parallel to the wave
PH.w: Sound is a longitudinal wave: molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

n.0: Waves carry energy, not matter; the molecules stay near their rest positions.
n.1: Circular motion of particles describes surface water waves, not sound.
n.2: Perpendicular motion describes a transverse wave such as light or a wave on a string.

PH.q: A 1,200 W hair dryer runs on a 120 V circuit. What current does it draw, and how much energy does it use in 0.50 h?

n.0: Inverts P / V (120 / 1,200).
n.1: Uses 1,200 W x 0.50 h = 600 Wh but labels it kWh.
n.3: Divides power by time (1,200 / 0.50) instead of multiplying.

PH.q: A 30 kg crate slides across a level floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Using g = 10 m/s², what friction force acts on it? (f = μN)
PH.w: Normal force on a level floor = weight = m g = 30 x 10 = 300 N. f = μN = 0.25 x 300 = 75 N.

n.0: Multiplies μ by the mass (0.25 x 30) and leaves out g.
n.1: Divides the normal force by μ (300 / 0.25) instead of multiplying.
n.3: 300 N is the normal force; it must be multiplied by μ.

PH.q: A 2.0 kg cart moving east at 4.0 m/s collides with a 2.0 kg cart moving west at 1.0 m/s, and they stick together. What is their velocity afterward?
PH.w: Take east as positive: total p = (2.0)(4.0) + (2.0)(-1.0) = 8.0 - 2.0 = 6.0 kg·m/s. v = 6.0 / 4.0 = 1.5 m/s, positive, so east.

n.1: Divides by one cart's mass (6.0 / 2.0); the joined mass is 4.0 kg.
n.2: Adds the momenta as if both carts moved east (10 / 4.0).
n.3: Gets the size right but the direction wrong; the eastward cart had more momentum.

PH.q: A rubber rod rubbed with fur becomes negatively charged. What happened?
o: Friction created new charge on the rod
Electrons moved from the rod to the fur
Electrons moved from the fur to the rod
Protons moved from the rod to the fur
PH.w: Rubbing transfers electrons. The rod gained electrons (negative) and the fur lost the same number (positive). Charge is conserved.

n.0: Charge is conserved: rubbing moves electrons but does not create charge.
n.1: Losing electrons would make the rod positive, not negative.
n.3: Protons stay in the nuclei; only electrons move when objects are charged.

PH.q: An orderly pushes an 80 kg loaded stretcher with a 200 N horizontal force. Friction on the wheels totals 40 N. What is the stretcher's acceleration?
PH.w: Net force = 200 N - 40 N = 160 N. a = F_net / m = 160 / 80 = 2.0 m/s².

n.1: Uses the applied force (200 / 80) instead of the net force; friction opposes the push.
n.2: Uses the friction force alone (40 / 80) as if it were the net force.
n.3: Adds friction to the push (240 / 80); friction acts against the motion.

PH.q: A cyclist slows steadily from 15 m/s to 3.0 m/s in 4.0 s. What is the cyclist's acceleration?
PH.w: a = (v - v0) / t = (3.0 - 15) / 4.0 = -12 / 4.0 = -3.0 m/s². The negative sign shows the cyclist is slowing.

n.0: Divides only the final speed by the time (3.0 / 4.0); acceleration uses the change in velocity.
n.2: Adds the speeds (15 + 3.0 = 18) instead of subtracting them.
n.3: Drops the sign; the velocity decreases, so the acceleration is opposite the motion (negative).

PH.q: A 720 N person stands on both feet with a total sole area of 0.030 m². What pressure do the feet exert on the floor?

n.0: Multiplies force by area (720 x 0.030); pressure divides force by area.
n.2: 48,000 Pa would be the pressure on one foot (half the area).
n.3: Halves the answer; both feet share the weight, but the area already includes both.

PH.q: An electric motor uses 2,500 J of electrical energy to do 2,000 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
PH.w: Efficiency = useful output / input x 100% = 2,000 / 2,500 x 100% = 80%.

n.0: 20% is the share wasted (500 / 2,500), not the efficiency.
n.1: Divides the wasted 500 J by the 2,000 J output.
n.3: Inverts the ratio; efficiency cannot exceed 100%.

PH.q: Two cars collide and crumple, and some kinetic energy becomes heat and sound. Assuming no external forces act, which quantity is conserved?
PH.w: In an inelastic collision of an isolated system, total momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some becomes heat, sound and deformation.

n.0: Both are conserved only in an elastic collision, where objects bounce without loss.
n.1: Reverses the rule: here kinetic energy is lost while momentum is kept.
n.2: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system.

PH.q: A ball is thrown straight up. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 9.8 m/s², what are its velocity and acceleration at the highest point?
PH.w: At the top the ball stops for an instant (v = 0), but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g = 9.8 m/s² downward the whole time.

n.0: Gravity accelerates the ball downward, not upward, at every point of the flight.
n.1: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration; gravity keeps pulling the ball down.
n.3: Swaps the two: the velocity is momentarily zero while the acceleration is 9.8 m/s².

PH.q: A cyclist takes the same curve at twice her earlier speed. By what factor does the centripetal force needed change?
PH.w: F_c = m v² / r depends on v², so doubling v multiplies the force by 2² = 4.

n.0: Faster on the same curve needs more inward force, not less.
n.1: Treats the force as proportional to v; it depends on v².
n.2: The force depends on speed; a faster turn needs more grip.

PH.q: Noise-canceling headphones make a sound wave that meets incoming noise crest to trough. Which wave behavior does this use?
PH.w: When a crest meets a trough the amplitudes cancel: destructive interference.

n.0: Diffraction is spreading around obstacles or through openings.
n.1: Resonance builds amplitude by driving an object at its natural frequency.
n.3: Constructive interference adds crests to crests and makes the sound louder.

PH.q: A nursing assistant finds that a heavy supply cart takes more force to start moving than to keep rolling at a steady speed. Which explains this?
o: The normal force drops once the cart moves
Maximum static friction exceeds kinetic friction
Kinetic friction exceeds maximum static friction
The cart's mass drops once it starts moving
PH.w: Static friction (surfaces not yet sliding) usually has a larger maximum than kinetic friction, so starting motion takes more force than maintaining it.

n.0: On a level floor the normal force equals the weight whether the cart is moving or not.
n.2: Reverses the rule: static friction's maximum is the larger one.
n.3: Mass is the amount of matter; it does not change when the cart moves.

PH.q: A sonar pulse returns to a boat 0.40 s after it is sent toward the seafloor. Sound travels at 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the water?
PH.w: Total path = 1,500 x 0.40 = 600 m, down and back. Depth = 600 / 2 = 300 m.

n.0: Divides speed by time (1,500 / 0.40) instead of multiplying.
n.1: Forgets to halve: 600 m is the round trip.
n.3: Halves twice; the 600 m round trip is halved once.

PH.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it moving just before it hits the ground?
PH.w: PE at the top becomes KE at the bottom: m g h = 1/2 m v², so v² = 2 g h = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 and v = 20 m/s.

n.1: Uses v² = g h (200) and drops the 2 from 1/2 m v².
n.2: Halves the correct speed; the energy equation gives 20 m/s.
n.3: Gives g h = 200 without the 2 or the square root.

PH.q: A 1,500 kg car accelerates at 2.0 m/s². What net force acts on the car?
PH.w: F_net = m a = 1,500 kg x 2.0 m/s² = 3,000 N.

n.0: Divides mass by acceleration (1,500 / 2.0); Newton's second law multiplies them.
n.1: Gives the mass value as if it were a force; it must be multiplied by the acceleration.
n.3: Computes the car's weight (1,500 x 10) instead of the net force for this acceleration.

PH.q: A nursing assistant pushes a supply cart 12 m along a hallway with a steady 25 N force in the direction of motion. How much work does she do on the cart?
PH.w: W = F d (force along the motion) = 25 N x 12 m = 300 J.

n.0: Halves the product; W = F d has no 1/2 factor.
n.1: Divides force by distance (25 / 12); work multiplies them.
n.2: Slips a decimal place (25 x 120).

PH.q: A ball rolls off a lab bench 1.25 m high at 2.0 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how far from the bench does it land? (fall distance = 1/2 gt²)
PH.w: Fall time: 1.25 = 1/2 x 10 x t², so t² = 0.25 and t = 0.50 s. Horizontal distance = 2.0 m/s x 0.50 s = 1.0 m.

n.0: Assumes a fall time of 1.0 s instead of solving for it.
n.2: Multiplies the speed by the height (2.0 x 1.25); distance needs the fall time.
n.3: Uses t² (0.25) as if it were t, giving 2.0 x 0.25 = 0.50 m.

PH.q: A server carries a 20 N tray 5.0 m across a level room at constant speed, holding it up with a 20 N upward force. How much work does the upward holding force do on the tray?
PH.w: Work is done only by a force component along the motion. The holding force is vertical and the motion is horizontal, so it does no work: 0 J.

n.1: Divides the force by the distance; and a perpendicular force does no work.
n.2: Halves 20 x 5.0; a force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
n.3: Multiplies the force by the distance even though the force is perpendicular to the motion.

PH.q: In a home, one lamp burns out but the other lamps on the same circuit stay lit. What does this show?
o: The lamps are wired in parallel
The current is used up in each lamp
The burned-out lamp had the least resistance
The lamps are wired in series

PH.w: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall with g, so they hit the ground together.
